# Validation

<!-- Made by scripts/gen_validation_doc.py from out/validation/validation.json; do not edit by hand. -->

Every model DexVantage computes is compared with an independent reference: a closed form written out again, another library, a published table, brute-force ray casting, Monte Carlo, or MuJoCo renders. This page is made from the report of a full run (`dexvantage --validate out/validation`, 2026-11-08 UTC, seed 20261027): **239 of 239 checks pass** over 38 models in 425 s. A check passes when its error is finite and at most its tolerance; each tolerance is stated with why it is that size.

The run: dexvantage 0.1.0rc1, python 3.14.4, numpy 2.5.4, scipy 1.18.1, opencv 5.0.0, mujoco 3.17.0, qt 6.12.0 on Linux x86_64; MuJoCo renders by NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080/PCIe/SSE2 (EGL).

Frame and units: world: the primary robot's base, REP-103 (x forward, y left, z up), metres; each check states its error's unit.

Limits: The suite checks the models against references for the cases it builds; it does not show that a model describes a real robot, lens or sensor. Monte Carlo checks are statistical: their tolerance is 4.5 standard errors of the estimated spread, at a fixed seed.

## Agreement with MuJoCo renders

The checks whose reference is a MuJoCo render: MuJoCo's own OpenGL renderer (segmentation, depth and colour images through EGL) of the same scene, cameras and joint states, against what DexVantage predicts without rendering (spec §9.1, §18). Measured agreement is reported as it came out, including where it is lower.

## Every check, by model

### Frames, poses and quaternions

Model `frames` (dexvantage.core.frames): 6 of 6 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `frames.quat_to_matrix` | Quaternion to rotation matrix | 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ | 1 × 10⁻¹² |  | pass |
| `frames.matrix_to_quat` | Rotation matrix to quaternion | 8.03 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | rad | pass |
| `frames.urdf_rpy` | URDF roll, pitch, yaw | 3.11 × 10⁻¹⁴ | 1 × 10⁻¹² |  | pass |
| `frames.optical_rep103` | REP-103 optical frame | 0 | 0 |  | pass |
| `frames.mujoco_quat` | MuJoCo quaternion order | 4.72 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻¹² |  | pass |
| `frames.pose_compose` | Pose composition and inverse | 3.11 × 10⁻¹⁵ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | m | pass |

- **`frames.quat_to_matrix`** — Quaternion to rotation matrix. *Compared:* largest element difference between DexVantage's rotation matrix and scipy's for the same quaternion. *Reference:* scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.from_quat(...).as_matrix() (scalar-last, the same order DexVantage stores) ([scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation), [shoemake1985](#ref-shoemake1985)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Double precision rounding is about 1e-16 per element; 1e-12 leaves room for the products.
- **`frames.matrix_to_quat`** — Rotation matrix to quaternion. *Compared:* largest angle between DexVantage's quaternion and scipy's for the same matrix, including half turns. *Reference:* scipy.spatial.transform.Rotation.from_matrix(...).as_quat() ([scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation), [shepperd1978](#ref-shepperd1978)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The angle of the relative rotation (scipy's magnitude, full precision near zero). The quaternion's sign is chosen with w ≥ 0, which the check also requires.
- **`frames.urdf_rpy`** — URDF roll, pitch, yaw. *Compared:* largest element difference between the rotation of an rpy triple and scipy's extrinsic x-y-z Euler rotation; and the round-trip angle error rpy → quaternion → rpy → quaternion. *Reference:* URDF's definition (roll about fixed x, then pitch about fixed y, then yaw about fixed z) as scipy from_euler('xyz', …), lowercase = extrinsic axes ([urdf](#ref-urdf), [scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation)).
- **`frames.optical_rep103`** — REP-103 optical frame. *Compared:* largest difference between the optical frame's axes, expressed in the camera body frame, and REP-103's definition (z forward = body x, x right = body −y, y down = body −z). *Reference:* REP-103 §"Suffix Frames", written out in the check ([rep103](#ref-rep103)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Exact: the axes are a signed permutation, so any difference beyond rounding is a wrong axis.
- **`frames.mujoco_quat`** — MuJoCo quaternion order. *Compared:* largest element difference between DexVantage's rotation matrix and MuJoCo's mju_quat2Mat after the (x, y, z, w) → (w, x, y, z) conversion. *Reference:* MuJoCo's own C routine mju_quat2Mat (the library DexVantage exports to) ([mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml)).
- **`frames.pose_compose`** — Pose composition and inverse. *Compared:* largest position difference (m) of points mapped through a chain of three poses and its inverse, against scipy rotations applied step by step. *Reference:* scipy Rotation.apply and vector addition, one link at a time ([scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation)).

### Robot kinematics

Model `kinematics` (dexvantage.core.robot): 11 of 11 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `kinematics.ik_round_trip` | IK round trip, 6-joint arm (full pose) | 9.97 × 10⁻⁵ | 1 × 10⁻⁴ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.ik_position_only` | IK round trip, 5-joint arm (position only) | 9.3 × 10⁻⁵ | 1 × 10⁻⁴ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.manipulability_2r` | Manipulability of a planar 2R arm | 1.13 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | m² | pass |
| `kinematics.collision_spheres` | Self-collision distance, two spheres | 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.collision_capsules` | Self-collision distance, two capsules | 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.fk_poe_mujoco` | Forward kinematics: MuJoCo against product of exponentials | 8.74 × 10⁻¹⁵ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.dh_ur5e` | UR5e against its standard DH closed form | 5.59 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.dh_panda` | Franka Panda against its modified DH (Craig) closed form | 6.33 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m | pass |
| `kinematics.jacobian_fd` | Jacobian against finite differences | 4.4 × 10⁻¹⁰ | 1 × 10⁻⁷ | m/rad | pass |
| `kinematics.jacobian_mujoco` | Jacobian: PoE against MuJoCo | 8.83 × 10⁻¹⁵ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | m/rad | pass |
| `kinematics.obstacle_distance` | Robot-to-obstacle distance (project objects and surfaces) | 2.57 × 10⁻⁷ | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | m | pass |

- **`kinematics.ik_round_trip`** — IK round trip, 6-joint arm (full pose). *Compared:* largest tool position error of the IK solution, recomputed independently, over random reachable targets; every target must be solved and its rotation error be within 1 mrad. *Reference:* the target itself: the pose of a random collision-free joint vector, by a product of exponentials written out in the check (Rodrigues' formula; no MuJoCo), which also recomputes the solution's pose ([wampler1986](#ref-wampler1986), [sugihara2011](#ref-sugihara2011), [liegeois1977](#ref-liegeois1977), [lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The tolerance is the solver's convergence tolerance (0.1 mm, 1 mrad): a solution reported as converged must meet it when its pose is computed by an independent route. The targets come from joint vectors inside the limits, so all are reachable and must be solved; MuJoCo's forward kinematics must also agree with the product of exponentials to 1e-12.
- **`kinematics.ik_position_only`** — IK round trip, 5-joint arm (position only). *Compared:* largest tool position error of the position-only IK solution, recomputed independently, over random reachable targets; every target must be solved. *Reference:* the target position, from a product of exponentials written out in the check (no MuJoCo) ([nakamura1986](#ref-nakamura1986), [lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* A 5-joint arm cannot set all six pose coordinates; the solver reaches the position and gets the orientation as close as it can (as the target came from a real pose of the arm, the orientation is often reached too, which the detail counts).
- **`kinematics.manipulability_2r`** — Manipulability of a planar 2R arm. *Compared:* largest difference between √det(J Jᵀ) of the tip's planar (x, y) Jacobian and the closed form, over random joint angles including the stretched and folded singularities. *Reference:* the closed form w = |l₁ l₂ sin q₂| (Yoshikawa 1985), written out in the check ([yoshikawa1985](#ref-yoshikawa1985)).
  *Tolerance and why:* MuJoCo's Jacobian is analytic, so agreement is to rounding (1e-12 m² for w of order 0.1 m²). The condition number is checked as well (relative error < 1e-6, away from the singularity, where it is infinite).
- **`kinematics.collision_spheres`** — Self-collision distance, two spheres. *Compared:* largest difference between the signed distance of two spheres on non-adjacent links and the analytic one, over random placements (overlapping ones included); the in-collision flag must agree with the sign. *Reference:* the analytic distance |c₁ − c₂| − r₁ − r₂, written out in the check ([mujoco_geomdistance](#ref-mujoco_geomdistance)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Sphere–sphere distance is closed form in MuJoCo as here, so agreement is to rounding.
- **`kinematics.collision_capsules`** — Self-collision distance, two capsules. *Compared:* largest difference between the signed distance of two capsules on non-adjacent links and the analytic one, over random placements (overlapping ones included); the in-collision flag must agree with the sign. *Reference:* the closest points of the two axis segments (Ericson 2005, §5.1.9) written out in the check, minus the radii ([mujoco_geomdistance](#ref-mujoco_geomdistance), [ericson2005](#ref-ericson2005)).
  *Tolerance and why:* MuJoCo's capsule–capsule routine is a closed form as well (the closest points of the two axis segments), so agreement is to rounding; 1e-9 m, as for the spheres, flags any wrong branch of the segment-parameter clamping, which shows as millimetres.
- **`kinematics.fk_poe_mujoco`** — Forward kinematics: MuJoCo against product of exponentials. *Compared:* largest link position difference (m) between MuJoCo's forward kinematics (RobotModel.fk) and the independent product-of-exponentials chain (PoEChain.fk) over random joint vectors, every link of every robot; the rotation difference (rad) must also be within 1e-9. *Reference:* core/robot/kinematics.py: its own XML reading (xml.etree), tree building and twist exponentials, no MuJoCo; the robots of the project and the five written in the check ([lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017), [mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml), [urdf](#ref-urdf)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both are double-precision products of about twenty rigid transforms, so rounding stays near 1e-15; 1e-9 leaves room for that while any convention error (an rpy order, a quaternion order, degrees for radians, a joint anchor) shows as 1e-3 or more. Robots the independent reader cannot read are listed, not compared.
- **`kinematics.dh_ur5e`** — UR5e against its standard DH closed form. *Compared:* largest position difference (m) of DH frames 1–6 between the closed-form product of Rz(θ) Tz(d) Tx(a) Rx(α) and both engines (MuJoCo and PoE) on a UR5e written from the same table as MJCF and as URDF; rotations within 1e-9 rad. *Reference:* Universal Robots' published UR5e DH table, the standard DH product written out in the check ([ur_dh](#ref-ur_dh), [dh1955](#ref-dh1955), [spong2006](#ref-spong2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The models are written from the DH figures in the check, so the only difference is the route (a hinge with an offset anchor and tilted axis in MJCF, a joint origin and fixed frames in URDF, against the DH product): agreement is to rounding, and 1e-9 m flags any convention slip.
- **`kinematics.dh_panda`** — Franka Panda against its modified DH (Craig) closed form. *Compared:* largest position difference (m) of frames 1–7 and the flange between the closed-form product of Rx(α) Tx(a) Rz(θ) Tz(d) and both engines on a Panda written from the same table as URDF; rotations within 1e-9 rad. *Reference:* Franka's published Panda DH table (Craig's convention), the modified DH product written out in the check ([franka_dh](#ref-franka_dh), [craig2005](#ref-craig2005)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Joint ranges are not part of this check: θ is drawn in [−π, π] for every joint. The flange at q = 0 is (0.088, 0, 0.926) m: x = 0.0825 − 0.0825 + 0.088, z = 0.333 + 0.316 + 0.384 − 0.107.
- **`kinematics.jacobian_fd`** — Jacobian against finite differences. *Compared:* largest element difference between the PoE chain's analytic Jacobian (twists moved by the adjoint) and central finite differences of its own forward kinematics, every link of the built-in robots. *Reference:* central differences, step 1e-6 rad or m, of PoEChain.fk; rotation by the log of R(q+h) R(q−h)ᵀ ([lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Central differences carry a truncation error of about h²/6 times the third derivative (1e-13 here) and a rounding error of about 1e-16/h = 1e-10; 1e-7 is well above both and well below any wrong column (of order the link lengths, 0.1 m).
- **`kinematics.jacobian_mujoco`** — Jacobian: PoE against MuJoCo. *Compared:* largest element difference between the PoE chain's world-frame Jacobian and MuJoCo's mj_jac (RobotModel.jacobian), at each link origin and at a random point fixed in each link, columns matched by joint name, every robot. *Reference:* MuJoCo mj_jac (another implementation of the same Jacobian) ([mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both are exact formulas in double precision; 1e-9 allows for rounding only. The offset point (up to 0.2 m from the link origin on each axis) exercises the point argument and the link-to-world rotation that the origin alone does not.
- **`kinematics.obstacle_distance`** — Robot-to-obstacle distance (project objects and surfaces). *Compared:* largest difference between env_distance (a sphere on a robot with a moved and rotated base, against a box, sphere, cylinder, convex mesh and table of the project) and the closed-form signed distance, over random joint positions, overlapping ones included; the nearest obstacle's name must match. *Reference:* the signed distance of a point to a box, sphere and cylinder, written out in the check, minus the sphere's radius ([mujoco_geomdistance](#ref-mujoco_geomdistance), [ericson2005](#ref-ericson2005)).
  *Tolerance and why:* MuJoCo measures sphere–box and sphere–sphere distances in closed form and sphere–cylinder and sphere–mesh through its convex solver (GJK, with EPA for penetration), whose convergence tolerance is far below a micrometre at these sizes; 1e-6 m is the solver's margin, while a wrong frame (the base pose, a quaternion order, a half-size taken for a full size) shows as centimetres.

### Lens projection and defocus

Model `optics` (dexvantage.core.optics): 10 of 10 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `optics.coverage_density_fd` | Coverage pixels per millimetre against OpenCV finite differences | 0.006458 | 0.01 | relative | pass |
| `optics.opencv_pinhole_brown` | Pinhole and Brown-Conrady projection | 1.82 × 10⁻¹² | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | px | pass |
| `optics.opencv_fisheye` | Kannala-Brandt (fisheye) projection | 5.68 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | px | pass |
| `optics.round_trip` | Unprojection inverts projection | 4.69 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | px | pass |
| `optics.from_fov` | A model fitted to a stated FOV reproduces it | 2.33 × 10⁻¹² | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | deg | pass |
| `optics.pixel_density` | Pixel density on a patch facing the camera | 8.2 × 10⁻⁹ | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | (relative) | pass |
| `optics.depth_of_field` | Thin-lens depth of field | 2.89 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ | (relative) | pass |
| `optics.blur_circle` | Thin-lens defocus blur disc | 1.07 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻¹¹ | (relative) | pass |
| `optics.mujoco_fiducial_masks` | Pinhole camera against MuJoCo-rendered fiducial masks | 0.07539 | 0.1 | px | pass |
| `optics.mujoco_fiducial_centres` | Pinhole projection of sphere centres against MuJoCo renders | 0.1671 | 0.3 | px | pass |

- **`optics.coverage_density_fd`** — Coverage pixels per millimetre against OpenCV finite differences. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the study's pixels per millimetre and √|det J| of cv2.projectPoints differentiated across a patch facing the camera, over seen voxels of the scripted scene. *Reference:* cv2.projectPoints (OpenCV), central differences with a 0.1 mm step across the line of sight ([opencv_calib3d](#ref-opencv_calib3d)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The study stores pixels per millimetre in steps of 0.01 px/mm, so a value of 0.5 px/mm or more is within 1 % of its exact figure; the finite differences are accurate to about 1e-8 at a 0.1 mm step. 1 % is the storage step and nothing else.
- **`optics.opencv_pinhole_brown`** — Pinhole and Brown-Conrady projection. *Compared:* largest pixel difference between CameraModel.project and cv2.projectPoints for the same K and D (no distortion, five-term and eight-term rational Brown-Conrady), random points in front of the camera. *Reference:* OpenCV cv2.projectPoints (calib3d), an independent implementation of the same model ([opencv_calib3d](#ref-opencv_calib3d), [brown1966](#ref-brown1966)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both evaluate the same polynomial in double precision; they differ only in the order of operations (about 1e-13 px at 1000 px). 1e-6 px is far below any convention error: a half-pixel shift, swapped p1/p2 or a mis-ordered k3 shows as 1e-3 px or more.
- **`optics.opencv_fisheye`** — Kannala-Brandt (fisheye) projection. *Compared:* largest pixel difference between CameraModel.project (model kb) and cv2.fisheye.projectPoints for the same K and D, random points up to 85° off the axis. *Reference:* OpenCV cv2.fisheye.projectPoints, an independent implementation of the same model ([opencv_fisheye](#ref-opencv_fisheye), [kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The same polynomial in θ evaluated twice in double precision; 1e-6 px leaves six orders of magnitude above rounding and catches any convention error (θ against atan(r), the order of the terms).
- **`optics.round_trip`** — Unprojection inverts projection. *Compared:* largest pixel error of project(unproject(pixel)) over random pixels of the image, for every model (pinhole, Brown-Conrady, Kannala-Brandt, equidistant, equisolid, stereographic); the ray angle error of unproject(project(ray)) for random rays landing on the image must also be below 1e-9 rad. *Reference:* the pixels themselves (and the rays themselves): an inverse is exact by definition ([hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004), [kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The Brown-Conrady and Kannala-Brandt inverses are iterative (Newton, converged to 1e-12 in normalised units, about 1e-9 px); 1e-6 px allows for the image scale. Pixels with no ray (a Brown-Conrady model folding back before the corner) are counted, not compared.
- **`optics.from_fov`** — A model fitted to a stated FOV reproduces it. *Compared:* largest difference between the field of view a CameraModel.from_fov model shows (fov_deg: edge to edge from its own unprojection) and the stated horizontal, vertical and diagonal angles, over every model and a range of image sizes and FOVs. *Reference:* the stated angles (for Kannala-Brandt, consistent H/V/D triples generated from pinhole, equisolid, equidistant and stereographic lenses written out in the check) ([kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006), [miyamoto1964](#ref-miyamoto1964)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The closed forms invert r(θ) exactly and the Kannala-Brandt fit passes through the stated points as constraints, so only rounding and the iterative inverse remain (about 1e-12°); 1e-6° is far below a datasheet's 0.1° rounding and catches an edge off by half a pixel (about 0.05° at 1000 px).
- **`optics.pixel_density`** — Pixel density on a patch facing the camera. *Compared:* largest relative difference between CameraModel.pixels_per_metre (closed form) and √|det J| of the 2 × 2 Jacobian of the projection of a small patch facing the camera, by central finite differences of project(); every model, points across the field, and tilted surfaces (normals). *Reference:* finite differences of the projection itself (an independent derivative) ([hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004), [kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Central differences with a step of 1e-5 of the range: truncation about 1e-10 relative, rounding about 1e-16 × 1000 px / 1e-5 ≈ 1e-8; 1e-6 leaves margin for both while any error in the closed form (a missing cos θ, the sin θ of the tangential direction) is 1e-2 or more away from the axis.
- **`optics.depth_of_field`** — Thin-lens depth of field. *Compared:* largest relative difference between depth_of_field (solved from the blur-disc equation) and the near and far limits from the hyperfocal distance H = f²/(N c) + f: near = s (H − f)/(H + s − 2f), far = s (H − f)/(H − s) (infinite from s ≥ H). *Reference:* the hyperfocal-distance formulae of photographic optics, written out again in the check ([ray2002](#ref-ray2002)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Two algebraic forms of the same thin-lens result; only rounding separates them (about 1e-15 relative). 1e-10 catches any slip in either.
- **`optics.blur_circle`** — Thin-lens defocus blur disc. *Compared:* largest relative difference between blur_circle_px and the blur disc from the thin-lens equation 1/f = 1/z + 1/v written out here (image distances v_s, v_z; disc A |v_z − v_s| / v_z on the sensor at v_s, A = f/N); and the blur at the depth-of-field limits must equal the circle of confusion. *Reference:* the Gaussian thin-lens equation and similar triangles, written out again in the check and evaluated in exact rational arithmetic ([ray2002](#ref-ray2002), [hecht2017](#ref-hecht2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The reference is computed in exact rational arithmetic (fractions.Fraction) from the same floating-point inputs, so the error is DexVantage's own rounding: a few 1e-16, amplified by s / |s − z| because the focus distance passes through a metre-to-millimetre conversion. Points within 0.1 % of the focus distance are moved to 0.1 % from it, bounding that to about 1e-13; 1e-11 leaves margin.
- **`optics.mujoco_fiducial_masks`** — Pinhole camera against MuJoCo-rendered fiducial masks. *Compared:* largest distance between the centroid of a sphere's MuJoCo segmentation mask and the centroid of the mask CameraModel predicts (pixel centres whose ray passes within the sphere's angular radius); three MuJoCo cameras (fovy; focal + sensorsize; focalpixel + principalpixel), 63 spheres each. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer (mujoco.Renderer, EGL, segmentation, no multi-sampling) on a scripted MJCF scene ([mujoco_camera](#ref-mujoco_camera), [mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both masks sample the same pixel centres, so they differ only where MuJoCo's drawn sphere (a 128 × 64 polygon mesh, inscribed in the sphere) or its rasteriser's edge rule decides a boundary pixel the other way. One such pixel moves the centroid of a 150–200 px mask by about (its distance from the centroid) / (mask area) ≈ 7 / 180 ≈ 0.04 px; 0.1 px allows two. A focal length 0.1 % off, or a principal point 0.1 px off, would show as more at the image edge (0.3 px for 0.1 % at 320 px from the centre). Every mask must be found and overlap its prediction by at least 95 % (intersection over union).
- **`optics.mujoco_fiducial_centres`** — Pinhole projection of sphere centres against MuJoCo renders. *Compared:* largest distance between the centroid of a sphere's MuJoCo segmentation mask and the centre of its image predicted by CameraModel.project (midway between the projections of the two tangent rays in the plane of the optical axis, which removes the perspective bias); same scene as optics.mujoco_fiducial_masks. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer (mujoco.Renderer, EGL, segmentation, no multi-sampling) on a scripted MJCF scene ([mujoco_camera](#ref-mujoco_camera), [mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The centroid of a mask sampled at pixel centres is not the centre of the ellipse it samples: for these 14 px fiducials the sampling error alone, measured on CameraModel's own predicted masks against the predicted centres, is reported as sampling_error_max_px (about 0.2 px). 0.3 px is that measured sampling error with the 0.1 px of the mask check added. Comparing with the projected sphere centre without the ellipse correction would add the perspective bias (perspective_bias_max_px), which grows with the angle from the axis and the sphere's size.

- **`occlusion.camview_vs_raycast`** — Camera view pixel distances against exact ray casting. *Compared:* fraction of sampled pixels (away from silhouettes) whose distance in the Camera view image differs from the exact first hit along the same lens ray by more than 1 mm, or where only one finds a surface; UR5e sample, every imager, a Brown and a fisheye lens, random arm poses. *Reference:* core/raycast.py first_hit (Möller–Trumbore through a uniform grid) along CameraModel.unproject rays ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both measure the distance to the same triangle's plane along the same lens ray, so away from silhouettes they agree to rounding. Near a silhouette the image answers for its pixel centre (pinhole) or for the nearest pixel of its base or cube image, so a ray grazing an edge may land on the other side: those are counted but not held against it (they must stay under 3 % of the pixels). Hits closer than 1 cm, where the two near-clip rules differ, are left out.
- **`occlusion.coverage_vs_raycast`** — Coverage shares against projection and exact ray casting. *Compared:* largest absolute difference of the task-volume shares (seen by ≥ 1 camera, by ≥ 2, and by each camera) between the coverage study and an independent path; scripted scene with a box, a cylinder, a table and three static cameras. *Reference:* pinhole projection written out from the stated FOV and core/raycast.visible_exact (Möller–Trumbore through a uniform grid), with the voxels inside the objects found by a test written out again ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The study judges occlusion per cube-map texel (2/n rad at a face centre) and the reference per exact ray, so voxels within about a texel of a silhouette may differ either way; the image edges are the same closed interval in both. Half a percent of the volume leaves room for those voxels and nothing else. Per voxel, the disagreement must stay under 2 %, the occlusion answers farther than two texels from a silhouette must agree but for 1e-3 (rounding at the near clip), and the in-image answers but for 1e-4 (a voxel centre exactly on an image edge).
- **`occlusion.texel_depth_exact`** — Cube-map texel depth against exact ray casting. *Compared:* fraction of sampled texels whose stored distance differs from the exact first hit along the texel-centre ray by more than 1 mm (or where only one of them finds a surface); UR5e sample, both cameras, random arm poses. *Reference:* core/raycast.py: Möller–Trumbore ray–triangle intersection through a uniform grid (Amanatides–Woo traversal) ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both compute the distance to the triangle plane along the same ray; a texel can differ only where its centre lies on an edge shared by two triangles at different depths (the rasteriser's edge rule against the ray test's), or by float32 rounding of the stored distance. 1e-3 of the texels leaves room for those edge ties and nothing else.
- **`occlusion.cube_vs_raycast`** — Cube-map visibility against exact ray casting. *Compared:* fraction of points (random in the task volume) whose cube-map visibility differs from exact ray casting and that are not within two texels of a silhouette; UR5e sample, both cameras, random arm poses. *Reference:* core/raycast.visible_exact (Möller–Trumbore through a uniform grid) and raycast.near_silhouette ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The cube map answers per texel (2/n rad at a face centre), so a point within about a texel of a silhouette may be judged by a ray that passes the edge on the other side; those are counted but not held against it (they must stay under 2 % of the points). Anywhere else the two must agree: 1e-3 leaves room for rounding at the near clip and nothing else.
- **`occlusion.samples_vs_raycast`** — Cube-map visibility on both samples against exact ray casting. *Compared:* fraction of random task-volume points whose cube-map visibility differs from exact ray casting, pooled over the SO-100 and UR5e samples, every camera, three arm poses and every cube-map backend available. *Reference:* core/raycast.visible_exact: Möller–Trumbore ray–triangle intersection through a uniform grid, sharing no code with either rasteriser; the tolerance is the measured share of points within half a texel diagonal of a silhouette ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The cube map answers per texel: a point is judged by the ray through its texel's centre, at most half a texel diagonal from its own line of sight (√2/n rad = 0.16° at a face centre for n = 512; less towards a face's edges). So a point can be judged wrongly only when an occluder's silhouette passes within that angle of it, and the tolerance is the share of points that close to a silhouette, measured on these scenes with raycast.near_silhouette (a subsample of 1,000 points per map; half_texel_band_fraction). Disagreements farther than a whole texel (2/n rad) from any silhouette are faults: at most 1e-3 of the points may be there.
- **`occlusion.mujoco_box_spheres`** — Visibility against MuJoCo segmentation: a box in front of spheres. *Compared:* fraction of target pixels (spheres and a back wall, behind a box) where our visibility of the back-projected pixel centre disagrees with MuJoCo's segmentation, away from silhouettes; agreement in % reported. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer (mujoco.Renderer, EGL): segmentation and depth from a camera in a scripted MJCF scene ([mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [mujoco_camera](#ref-mujoco_camera), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Error: the share of target pixels where a cube map (or exact ray casting) disagrees with MuJoCo's segmentation and that are not within a texel (2/n rad) of a silhouette; those are faults, and 1e-3 leaves room for depth-buffer rounding of the back-projected points and nothing else. Near silhouettes the cube map answers per texel, coarser than the camera's pixels, so overall agreement must be at least 99 % for every backend; the agreement percentages are reported as measured.
- **`occlusion.mujoco_ur5e`** — Visibility against MuJoCo segmentation: the UR5e over a table. *Compared:* fraction of target pixels (the table top and spheres in the task volume, seen from above past the posed UR5e + 2F-85) where our visibility of the back-projected pixel centre disagrees with MuJoCo's segmentation, away from silhouettes; agreement in % reported. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer (mujoco.Renderer, EGL): segmentation and depth of the same MJCF file, posed by MuJoCo's own kinematics ([mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [mujoco_camera](#ref-mujoco_camera), [mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Error: the share of target pixels where a cube map (or exact ray casting) disagrees with MuJoCo's segmentation and that are not within a texel (2/n rad) of a silhouette; those are faults, and 1e-3 leaves room for depth-buffer rounding of the back-projected points and nothing else. Near silhouettes the cube map answers per texel, coarser than the camera's pixels, so overall agreement must be at least 99 % for every backend; the agreement percentages are reported as measured. Measured with the default seed: 4 of about 163,000 target pixels disagree away from every silhouette, for exact ray casting and both cube maps alike. Three are single pixels inside a robot mesh where MuJoCo's rasteriser leaves a crack between two triangles and shows the table through it (our ray hits the mesh there); one lies on the table's own edge, where the two renders (with and without the robot, so with different depth ranges) round the edge differently.

- **`grasp.tcp_vs_pinch_site`** — Tool centre of the Robotiq 2F-85 against the model's pinch site. *Compared:* angle between the approach axis measured from the pads and the line from the gripper frame to the file's "pinch" site; the TCP must lie within 1 mm of that line. *Reference:* the gripper_pinch site of MuJoCo Menagerie's robotiq_2f85 (on the gripper's axis of symmetry) ([mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The pads are mirror images about the axis on which the file puts the pinch site, so the measured axis should match it to rounding; 0.5° is 1.3 mm over the 145 mm to the site. The TCP is the pads' centre, 14 mm short of the pinch site (which sits at the pads' tips).
- **`grasp.sampler_closed_form`** — Grasp samplers against their closed forms. *Compared:* largest deviation of a sampled grasp from its kind's closed form (TCP height above the table and footprint, approach direction, heading spread, closing axis), the pose read back with SciPy's Rotation. *Reference:* the samplers' definitions written out again; SciPy's quaternion-to-matrix conversion ([scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation), [rep103](#ref-rep103)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Every quantity is a closed form of the sampler's definition; the only rounding is double precision through a quaternion (about 1e-15), so 1e-9 catches any frame or sign mistake.
- **`grasp.object_points_box`** — Points on a task object's surface. *Compared:* largest |signed distance| of object_points on a rotated box from the box's surface; each face's share of the points must be within 4σ (binomial) of its share of the area. *Reference:* the closed-form signed distance of a box, written out in the check.
  *Tolerance and why:* Points are drawn on the box's own triangles, so their distance to the surface is rounding (1e-17 m); a wrong pose or size shows as centimetres. 4σ keeps the area test from failing by chance (about 1 in 16 000 per face) while a sampler ignoring area is off by tens of σ.
- **`grasp.trajectory_closures`** — Grasps found where the gripper closes in a trajectory. *Compared:* largest |opening − the distance between the pads' inner-face centres| over the trajectory's samples (m); the strokes found must be the script's closing ranges, sample for sample. *Reference:* the 2F-85 pads' inner faces built from MuJoCo's compiled box geoms (mj_kinematics on a fresh MjData); the sample ranges the scripted trajectory closes the fingers over ([mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The pads are rigid boxes, so the opening is exact up to float32 meshes (about 3e-8 m); picking the wrong face or link shows as millimetres. The strokes are exact: the script holds the fingers still between its ramps.

### Rendered against predicted (MuJoCo ground truth)

Model `groundtruth` (dexvantage.core.sim, dexvantage.core.studies.groundtruth): 6 of 6 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `groundtruth.lens_remap_fiducials` | Distortion remap against the lens model, six lens models | 0.2011 | 0.4 | px | pass |
| `groundtruth.scene_intrinsics` | Scene cameras against the sensors' lens models | 8.8 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.001 | px | pass |
| `groundtruth.scene_vs_camrender` | MuJoCo segmentation against the Camera view's rasteriser | 2.2 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.001 | fraction of pixels | pass |
| `groundtruth.ur5e_contacts` | Predicted against rendered contact visibility, UR5e sample | 0.07246 | 0.15 | fraction of points | pass |
| `groundtruth.ur5e_depth` | Predicted depth validity against rendered depth, UR5e sample | 0.002227 | 0.01 | fraction of voxels | pass |
| `groundtruth.synthetic_roundtrip` | Synthetic LeRobot episodes read back | 0 | 0 | mismatches | pass |

- **`groundtruth.lens_remap_fiducials`** — Distortion remap against the lens model, six lens models. *Compared:* largest distance between the centroid of a sphere's rendered mask (MuJoCo segmentation remapped through CameraModel by core/sim/render.py) and the centroid of the mask CameraModel predicts (pixel centres whose ray lies within the sphere's angular radius); 35 spheres per lens model, six models. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer through EGL on a scripted scene of spheres, the pinhole renders resampled with cv2.remap ([mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317), [mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [opencv_remap](#ref-opencv_remap), [kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both masks sample the same pixel centres through the same rays, so they differ only where a boundary pixel goes the other way: MuJoCo draws a sphere as a 128 × 64 polygon mesh (0.10 px measured on the pinhole, as in optics.mujoco_fiducial_masks), and the remap samples the base image at its nearest pixel, which moves a boundary by up to half a base pixel; the base is at least twice as dense as the lens image (render.OVERSAMPLE = 2, a default), so that is at most a quarter of a lens pixel at a boundary and less on a centroid of about 110 pixels (measured up to 0.33 px with OVERSAMPLE = 1). 0.4 px allows both; a principal point off by a pixel, a focal length off by 0.3 %, a wrong remap direction or a wrong cube face would each show as one pixel or more. The centroid against CameraModel.project of the centre (centre_vs_project_max_px) adds the sphere image's own offset from its centre's projection. Every mask must be found and overlap its prediction by at least 85 % (IoU; a 6 px sphere has about 110 pixels, 38 of them on its boundary).
- **`groundtruth.scene_intrinsics`** — Scene cameras against the sensors' lens models. *Compared:* largest difference in fx, fy, cx or cy (px) between each MuJoCo scene camera, read back from the compiled model (cam_intrinsic, cam_sensorsize; the principal offset's measured sign), and its imager's CameraModel; every imager of the UR5e, SO-100 and dexhand samples. *Reference:* the compiled MuJoCo model (mujoco.MjSpec.compile of the camera's sensorsize, focalpixel, principalpixel and resolution) ([mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317)).
  *Tolerance and why:* MuJoCo stores the intrinsics as float32 lengths (cam_intrinsic = focalpixel · sensorsize / resolution): a relative rounding of 6 × 10⁻⁸ on a focal length of 1 400 px is 10⁻⁴ px. 10⁻³ px allows that; a principal point taken with the wrong sign is off by twice its offset.
- **`groundtruth.scene_vs_camrender`** — MuJoCo segmentation against the Camera view's rasteriser. *Compared:* share of pixels whose owner (robot link, object, surface or nothing) differs between MuJoCo's segmentation of each sample camera (core/sim/render.py) and core/camrender's rasterisation of the same scene at the home pose; every camera of the UR5e, SO-100 and dexhand samples at half their stream size. *Reference:* MuJoCo's OpenGL renderer through EGL (segmentation, no multi-sampling) on the scene built by core/sim/scene.py ([mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both sample each pixel at its centre (MuJoCo with multi-sampling off), so a pixel differs only where a triangle edge passes within rounding of a pixel centre and the two edge rules (OpenGL's top-left rule, camrender's inclusive test) decide it differently: a few pixels per image (measured 0 to 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ of the pixels). 10⁻³ allows that; a camera off by a pixel, or a link at the wrong pose, would differ along every edge (about 10⁻² here). Where the owners agree, at most 10⁻³ of the pixels may differ in range along the pixel ray by more than 1 mm (they agree to float32 rounding except where a pixel sees one link's silhouette through two of its triangles, up to 9 mm on the SO-100's third-person camera).
- **`groundtruth.ur5e_contacts`** — Predicted against rendered contact visibility, UR5e sample. *Compared:* 1 − the agreement of the grasp study's predicted contact-point visibility with the rendered one (contact points in view, both cameras, home, a 50-grasp sample of the set (10 in a quick run) and 8 frames of the scripted pick trajectory); also at most 2% of them may disagree on occlusion away from an edge, on the UR5e and on the SO-100 sample (whose agreement is reported beside it, not held to the floor). *Reference:* MuJoCo segmentation and depth of the same scene and joint states (core/studies/groundtruth.py) ([mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The floor is 85% agreement (measured 92.8 % over home, 50 grasps and 8 trajectory frames: the grasps 91.1 %, the trajectory frames 98.9 %): most disagreements are points within a pixel of a segmentation edge (the overhead camera sees the pads nearly edge-on) or a difference of rule (the prediction tests the contact location 2 mm in front of the pad, the render the pad face); those are reported, not hidden. Occlusion disagreements away from an edge must stay under 2% of the points (measured 0.4 %): more would mean the prediction's scene or cube maps differ from the render. The SO-100 sample reads 84.2 % here, not held to this floor (its jaws' contact patches come from collision geometry off the visual mesh, so its rule disagreements are larger); it is held to the same occlusion limit (0.4 % measured) and its agreement is in the detail, not hidden.
- **`groundtruth.ur5e_depth`** — Predicted depth validity against rendered depth, UR5e sample. *Compared:* 1 − the agreement of the depth-validity study's voxels (valid or not) with the rendered depth of every imager the depth needs, the reference depth with the sensor's noise model added; both depth sensors of the UR5e sample at home. *Reference:* MuJoCo depth renders of the same scene (core/studies/groundtruth.py) ([mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer), [intel_d400](#ref-intel_d400)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The floor is 99% of the voxels (measured 99.8 %). Field of view, min-Z, range, projector and materials are the same functions on both sides; what is compared is the study's cube-map occlusion from both imagers against the rendered depth, and the noise, which moves voxels within a few σ_z of a surface. On the surfaces themselves (reported, not checked) the agreement is lower (92 % for the overhead D435): a point exactly on a surface is where a cube-map texel's 1 mm tolerance is weakest.
- **`groundtruth.synthetic_roundtrip`** — Synthetic LeRobot episodes read back. *Compared:* number of mismatches when two synthetic SO-100 episodes (every fault on, 64 × 48 px) written as LeRobot v2.1 and v3.0 are read back: columns not bit-exact after the float32 cast, frame counts, camera times off by more than half a 90 kHz tick, frames below 30 dB PSNR or closer to a neighbour, duplicates not repeating their frame within 30 dB, gaps not where the sidecar says, a sidecar that differs from the generator's. *Reference:* the generator's own arrays (joint states, actions, stamps, the frames before encoding) and the ground truth it returned, against the dataset read back through core/datasets (the LeRobot reader, checked independently by formats.lerobot_roundtrip) ([lerobot_dataset_format](#ref-lerobot_dataset_format), [mujoco_renderer](#ref-mujoco_renderer)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The faults are injected by the generator itself and recorded in the sidecar; this check confirms the files carry exactly them. Finding them from the data alone is the auditor's job (spec §8.2).

| `handeye.closed_form_noisy` | Closed-form hand-eye solvers on noisy views | 5.874 | 15 | mm | pass |
| `handeye.ba_truth` | Bundle adjustment against the truth | 3.111 | 5 | σ | pass |
| `handeye.ba_covariance_mc` | Bundle-adjustment covariance against Monte Carlo | 0.5577 | 1 | of the band | pass |
| `handeye.axzb_two_arms` | AX = ZB with both sides moving | 3.501 | 15 | mm | pass |
| `handeye.charuco_render` | ChArUco detection on rendered boards | 0.113 | 0.25 | px | pass |
| `handeye.aprilgrid_render` | AprilGrid detection on rendered boards | 0.1181 | 0.25 | px | pass |
| `handeye.planner_vs_ba` | Planned covariance against the bundle adjustment | 0.008734 | 0.09531 | ln ratio | pass |
| `handeye.sessions_joint` | Two capture sessions in one bundle adjustment | 1.281 | 5 | σ | pass |
| `handeye.silhouette_recovery` | Silhouette calibration recovers a known mount slip | 1.659 | 2 | px | pass |
| `handeye.silhouette_vs_board` | Silhouette calibration against the board-based hand-eye solve | 1.647 | 2 | px | pass |

- **`handeye.dataset_capture`** — Hand-eye calibration from a recorded LeRobot episode. *Compared:* distance of the calibrated camera from the mount the frames were rendered through (mm); its rotation must also be within 0.05°. *Reference:* the true mount: the project's mount moved by simcapture's default offset (2.06 mm, 0.62°), through which the board images were rendered ([lerobot_dataset_format](#ref-lerobot_dataset_format), [opencv_charuco](#ref-opencv_charuco), [park_martin1994](#ref-park_martin1994)).
  *Tolerance and why:* 0.2 mm and 0.05°: the error is 3-4 times the solver's own σ even on uncoded frames at full size (0.020 mm against σ 0.006 mm, measured: the corner errors of a rendered view are not independent, as σ assumes); half the stream size doubles the corner error in the sensor's pixels and AV1 coding adds under 0.002 mm. The camera starts 2.7 mm and 0.62° away; joints read at the wrong frames or corners left in the stream's pixels miss by millimetres.
- **`handeye.closed_form_exact`** — Closed-form hand-eye solvers on exact poses. *Compared:* largest translation error (m) of X and Z from each closed-form method (five AX = XB, two AX = ZB) on exact board poses, eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand on the UR5e sample; every rotation error must be below 1e-9 rad. *Reference:* the ground-truth transforms the poses were generated from ([tsai_lenz1989](#ref-tsai_lenz1989), [park_martin1994](#ref-park_martin1994), [horaud_dornaika1995](#ref-horaud_dornaika1995), [andreff1999](#ref-andreff1999), [daniilidis1999](#ref-daniilidis1999), [opencv_handeye](#ref-opencv_handeye), [shah2013](#ref-shah2013), [li2010](#ref-li2010)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Every method is exact on noise-free motions; what is left is rounding (about 1e-15 m). 1e-9 m fails any convention error (a transform inverted or A and B swapped gives errors of centimetres to metres). Backend "numpy": the NumPy versions in core/calib/axxb.py, because this OpenCV has no calibrateHandEye in its Python bindings.
- **`handeye.closed_form_noisy`** — Closed-form hand-eye solvers on noisy views. *Compared:* largest translation error (mm) of X from each closed-form method on board poses from PnP on corners with 0.3 px noise (20 poses, eye-in-hand and eye-to-hand, several seeds); every rotation error must be below 1.5°. *Reference:* the ground-truth camera pose ([tsai_lenz1989](#ref-tsai_lenz1989), [park_martin1994](#ref-park_martin1994), [horaud_dornaika1995](#ref-horaud_dornaika1995), [andreff1999](#ref-andreff1999), [daniilidis1999](#ref-daniilidis1999), [opencv_handeye](#ref-opencv_handeye), [shah2013](#ref-shah2013), [li2010](#ref-li2010), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The closed-form methods solve algebraic errors on PnP poses that are each a few tenths of a millimetre off, so they are not exact; on these scenes their errors were 3–8 mm and up to 0.6° when the tolerance was set. 15 mm and 1.5° leave margin over that spread and still fail a convention error (tens of millimetres to tens of degrees). Tsai-Lenz is singular for a camera rotation of 180°; the eye-to-hand scene's camera is at 151°.
- **`handeye.ba_truth`** — Bundle adjustment against the truth. *Compared:* largest error of any estimated quantity (X, Z, intrinsics, determined joint offsets) in units of its own predicted σ, on eye-in-hand, eye-to-hand, two-camera, intrinsics, encoder-noise and joint-offset scenes (0.3 px noise); the translation errors must also stay below 1 mm for the wrist and held-board transforms. *Reference:* the ground truth the corners were generated from ([triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* With Gaussian corner noise an unbiased estimate is within about 3σ in each component almost always; 5σ over the few tens of components checked is passed by chance with probability below 1e-5, while a biased model (a frame convention, a wrong FK link, a pixel-centre error) is off by tens to thousands of σ. In the joint-offset scene the first and last joints' offsets are not determined by the views (they trade off against Z and X about the same axes); only the determined offsets are compared there.
- **`handeye.ba_covariance_mc`** — Bundle-adjustment covariance against Monte Carlo. *Compared:* largest share of the χ² band used by the ratio empirical σ / predicted σ over the 12 components of X and Z (ln ratio over ln of the band edge on its side; 1 = at the edge), the empirical σ the RMS error about the truth over noise draws (same poses, 0.5 px), the predicted σ the RMS of the per-draw Gauss-Newton σ, the band the 99 % χ² interval of the number of draws (Bonferroni over the 12 components). *Reference:* a Monte Carlo simulation of the corner noise ([triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* With n draws the empirical σ of an unbiased Gaussian estimate scatters about the true σ by the χ² law with n degrees of freedom; the band holds 99 % of that scatter for each of the 12 components together. A covariance missing the residual variance, or J built at the wrong point, is off by factors of 2 or more.
- **`handeye.axzb_two_arms`** — AX = ZB with both sides moving. *Compared:* largest translation difference (mm) between the bundle adjustment's X and Z and the closed-form robot-world solvers' (Shah, Li) on a camera on one UR5e seeing a board held by a second (20 poses, 0.3 px); the bundle adjustment must also be within 5σ of the truth. *Reference:* OpenCV calibrateRobotWorldHandEye when installed, else the NumPy Shah and Li solvers; and the ground truth ([shah2013](#ref-shah2013), [li2010](#ref-li2010), [opencv_handeye](#ref-opencv_handeye), [triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The closed-form solvers start from PnP poses and minimise algebraic errors, so they differ from the bundle adjustment by the order of their own error (a few millimetres here); the tolerance is that of handeye.closed_form_noisy. The bundle adjustment itself is held to the truth within 5σ, as in handeye.ba_truth.
- **`handeye.charuco_render`** — ChArUco detection on rendered boards. *Compared:* largest per-view RMS (px) between the detected ChArUco corners and the true corners projected through the camera model, on boards rendered at known poses (0.38–0.6 m, up to 40° of tilt, 1 grey level of noise) through a Brown-Conrady camera; the PnP pose must be within 1 mm and 0.2° and half the corners found. *Reference:* the known board pose, projected through the same camera model ([garrido2014](#ref-garrido2014), [opencv_charuco](#ref-opencv_charuco), [opencv_calib3d](#ref-opencv_calib3d), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Sub-pixel corner detectors locate sharp chessboard corners to about a tenth of a pixel; 0.25 px fails a half-pixel convention error, a wrong board layout or a wrong corner order (a pixel or more). The renderer integrates each pixel over 3 × 3 rays, so the corners carry the area coverage a sensor sees.
- **`handeye.aprilgrid_render`** — AprilGrid detection on rendered boards. *Compared:* largest per-view RMS (px) between the detected AprilGrid tag corners (Kalibr layout, corner squares) and the true corners projected through the camera model, as handeye.charuco_render. *Reference:* the known board pose, projected through the same camera model ([wang_olson2016](#ref-wang_olson2016), [kalibr](#ref-kalibr), [opencv_charuco](#ref-opencv_charuco), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* With Kalibr's corner squares every tag corner is a chessboard-like X corner, which the sub-pixel step locates without bias; 0.25 px as for ChArUco.
- **`handeye.planner_vs_ba`** — Planned covariance against the bundle adjustment. *Compared:* largest |ln(σ_BA / σ_plan)| over the 12 components of X and Z: σ_plan the pose planner's predicted 1σ at the planned poses (15, UR5e sample, eye-in-hand, the sample's wrist camera, the default ChArUco board, 0.5 px), σ_BA the bundle adjustment's 1σ from corners simulated at the same poses with 0.5 px Gaussian noise (the same corner ids), σ estimated from its residuals. *Reference:* the bundle adjustment of core/calib/handeye.py (an independent Jacobian, by central differences of its residuals, linearised at its own estimate) ([triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both are the Gauss-Newton covariance of the same estimator, so they agree when the planner's Jacobian is right; they differ by the bundle adjustment's σ̂ (its relative scatter is 1/√(2·dof), 2.3 % here, 3 × that within the tolerance) and by linearising at its estimate instead of the truth (far smaller at 0.5 px). With σ̂ / σ taken out the ratios must agree within 0.01 in ln (the shape of the covariance). A wrong sign, frame or missing rotation coupling in the planner gives factors of 2 or more. The bundle adjustment's covariance is itself held to a Monte Carlo spread by handeye.ba_covariance_mc.
- **`handeye.sessions_joint`** — Two capture sessions in one bundle adjustment. *Compared:* largest error of a calibrated mount (the wrist camera eye-in-hand; the overhead camera, fixed, seeing the same fixed board, located only through it) against the truth, per translation axis in units of its own predicted σ; the overhead camera starts 10 mm off. *Reference:* the ground-truth mounts the corners were generated from (0.2 px noise) ([triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000), [hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Errors of an unbiased estimator are within 5σ with probability above 99.9 % per component; a camera located through the wrong board pose, or a shared board estimated twice, shows as its 10 mm start offset, many σ away.
- **`handeye.silhouette_recovery`** — Silhouette calibration recovers a known mount slip. *Compared:* largest error, in pixels of the 640 px working image (position over a pixel's width at the robot's depth, rotation over a pixel's angle), of a static camera's optical frame recovered from the robot's silhouette in synthetic LeRobot episodes (MuJoCo renders, 640 × 360, AV1), before and after a slip of 5 mm and 1° (a default of this check), on the SO-100 third-person and UR5e overhead cameras; every estimate must be observable and the slip found as a step between the episodes. *Reference:* the true mount in the generator's ground-truth sidecar, read only after the estimate ([barrow1977](#ref-barrow1977), [borgefors1988](#ref-borgefors1988), [canny1986](#ref-canny1986), [liu2010_fdcm](#ref-liu2010_fdcm), [opencv_distance_transform](#ref-opencv_distance_transform), [efron1979](#ref-efron1979), [liang_zeger1986](#ref-liang_zeger1986), [mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317)).
  *Tolerance and why:* so100 (Third-person camera (sample placement)): episode 0 1.65 px (2.39 mm, 0.299°), episode 1 1.66 px (2.16 mm, 0.301°); ur5e (Overhead D435): episode 0 1.13 px (1.28 mm, 0.031°), episode 1 0.32 px (0.37 mm, 0.026°); rendered on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5080/PCIe/SSE2
- **`handeye.silhouette_vs_board`** — Silhouette calibration against the board-based hand-eye solve. *Compared:* difference, in pixels of the 640 px working image (as handeye.silhouette_recovery), between the static camera's optical frame from the silhouette calibration (the slipped episode of the synthetic SO-100 dataset) and from the board-based bundle adjustment of a simulated ChArUco capture (15 planned poses) of the same rig with the same slip; the board solve must be within 0.5 mm and 0.05° of the truth. *Reference:* the board-based hand-eye bundle adjustment (core/calib/handeye.py) on the same synthetic rig ([barrow1977](#ref-barrow1977), [borgefors1988](#ref-borgefors1988), [canny1986](#ref-canny1986), [liu2010_fdcm](#ref-liu2010_fdcm), [opencv_distance_transform](#ref-opencv_distance_transform), [efron1979](#ref-efron1979), [liang_zeger1986](#ref-liang_zeger1986), [mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317), [triggs2000](#ref-triggs2000), [garrido2014](#ref-garrido2014)).
  *Tolerance and why:* silhouette 1.65 px (2.12 mm, 0.299°) from the board solve; the board solve 0.039 mm and 0.0047° from the truth

### Motion blur, time sync and action-chunk latency

Model `timing` (dexvantage.core.studies.motion_blur, dexvantage.core.studies.time_sync, dexvantage.core.studies.action_chunk_sync): 7 of 7 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `blur.image_velocity_fd` | Image-plane velocity against finite differences of projected points | 2.84 × 10⁻⁹ | 1 × 10⁻⁵ | fraction | pass |
| `blur.smear_analytic` | Smear of a point moving parallel to the image plane against f·v·E/Z | 2.36 × 10⁻¹¹ | 1 × 10⁻⁶ | fraction | pass |
| `blur.rolling_shutter_bruteforce` | Rolling-shutter capture against a row-by-row simulation | 0.02381 | 0.05 | fraction | pass |
| `chunk.loop_vs_simulation` | Action-chunk loop against a discrete-time simulation of a moving point | 2.91 × 10⁻⁵ | 5 × 10⁻⁵ | m | pass |
| `chunk.ensemble_closed_form` | Temporal ensembling against the closed-form weighted average | 3.27 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | steps | pass |
| `sync.stamp_interval_sim` | Stamp-error interval against a simulation of the frame timeline | 3.47 × 10⁻¹⁸ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | s | pass |
| `sync.action_label_sim` | Action-label error against a simulated moving end effector | 2.21 × 10⁻⁴ | 0.02 | fraction | pass |

- **`blur.image_velocity_fd`** — Image-plane velocity against finite differences of projected points. *Compared:* largest |(u̇, v̇)_study − (u̇, v̇)_fd| over the points in view, as a share of that frame's largest image speed. *Reference:* central differences (h = 10 µs) of the points projected through the lens at q(t ± h): forward kinematics of the camera's link and of the gripper's links, no Jacobian ([mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [lynch_park2017](#ref-lynch_park2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Central differences are exact to O(h²): at h = 10 µs the truncation is far below 10⁻⁸ of the speed and the rounding of uv (about 10⁻¹³ px) over 2h is about 10⁻⁸ px/s, so 10⁻⁵ of the peak speed leaves room for both while a wrong frame, sign or lever arm shows as a share near 1.
- **`blur.smear_analytic`** — Smear of a point moving parallel to the image plane against f·v·E/Z. *Compared:* largest relative difference of the smear (px) from the closed forms f·v·E/Z (translation) and f·ω·E (a camera turning about its own y axis, a point on the axis). *Reference:* the pinhole relation u = fx·X/Z + cx differentiated by hand; the Kannala-Brandt lens has r = f·θ near the axis ([hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004), [kannala_brandt2006](#ref-kannala_brandt2006)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The pinhole derivative is exact, so the difference is rounding (10⁻¹⁵); the fisheye's derivative is a central difference with a step of 10⁻⁶ of the distance, accurate to about 10⁻¹⁰; 10⁻⁶ leaves room for both.
- **`blur.rolling_shutter_bruteforce`** — Rolling-shutter capture against a row-by-row simulation. *Compared:* largest distance between where the study puts a moving point in a rolling-shutter image and where a row-by-row simulation of the readout finds it, as a share of how far the point moved during the readout. *Reference:* a brute-force readout: row r is read at readout · r/(H − 1); each point is projected at the robot's true pose at every row time (forward kinematics along the trajectory) and caught where its image crosses the row being read ([liang2008](#ref-liang2008)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The study takes the image motion as linear over the readout; the simulation follows the true motion (the camera turning, the perspective changing), so they differ at second order: ½·ü·t² against u̇·t, a share ü·t/(2·u̇) of how far the point moved (at least 1 px is used), a few per cent for a wrist camera over a 30 ms readout. 5 % allows that; a wrong row time, direction or sign moves the point by a share near 1.
- **`chunk.loop_vs_simulation`** — Action-chunk loop against a discrete-time simulation of a moving point. *Compared:* the largest of |mean(simulated) − mean(model)| and the simulated closes outside the model's interval, position error of a point at 0.1 m/s, over four loop scenarios (host and mid-exposure stamps, skipped actions, a command latency that differs from the recording's). *Reference:* event-by-event simulation of frames, inference starts, chunk indexing and control ticks (20 000 trials each) ([zhao2023_act](#ref-zhao2023_act), [act_code](#ref-act_code)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The simulation plays the events (frames on their own clock, the newest frame ready at inference start, the chunk index rounded to whole steps, the next control tick); the model adds the terms with their ranges.
- **`chunk.ensemble_closed_form`** — Temporal ensembling against the closed-form weighted average. *Compared:* largest difference, in control steps, between the lag of ACT's step-by-step ensemble of a moving point (and ensemble_mean_age) and the geometric-series closed form; and between the ensembled vector and Σ wᵢ aᵢ / Σ wᵢ. *Reference:* the closed form of exp(−m·i) weights, i = 0 the oldest (ACT code) ([zhao2023_act](#ref-zhao2023_act), [act_code](#ref-act_code), [lerobot_act_ensembler](#ref-lerobot_act_ensembler)).
  *Tolerance and why:* i = 0 is the oldest prediction, as in ACT's code; a negative m weights the newest more.
- **`sync.stamp_interval_sim`** — Stamp-error interval against a simulation of the frame timeline. *Compared:* largest amount (s) by which a simulated stamp error falls outside the study's interval, or by which the study's USB transfer times differ from the frame sizes and capacity typed in again; the simulated errors must also span at least 90 % of each interval. *Reference:* a frame simulated row by row (exposure and readout), queued behind a random set of other frames on a USB 3.2 Gen 1 bus (450 MB/s), seen at the next 125 µs bus interval; device clocks read at a random instant of the exposure with offset, jitter and drift drawn over their stated ranges ([usb32_spec](#ref-usb32_spec), [usb20_spec](#ref-usb20_spec), [ms_usb_isoch](#ref-ms_usb_isoch), [liang2008](#ref-liang2008)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both sides add the same physical terms, so a stamp outside the interval is a term the study misses or a wrong sign; 10⁻⁹ s is rounding. The span condition shows the interval is not wider than the timeline allows (each term is drawn at its ends a third of the time, so the extremes are reached).
- **`sync.action_label_sim`** — Action-label error against a simulated moving end effector. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the study's action-label error and the largest error in a simulation that stamps 30 fps frames with the skew. *Reference:* frames at random phases along the UR5e sample's scripted pick; the label is the TCP at the stamp, the truth the TCP at the exposure, each by forward kinematics at that instant (no grid, no interpolation) ([mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The study takes the largest displacement over every instant (a 1 ms path, linear between); the simulation only sees the frames it samples, so it can fall a little short of the largest displacement, and the path's chords differ from the arc by far less than a micrometre. 2 % allows the sampling; a skew applied with the wrong sign or scale shows as tens of per cent.

### Bandwidth, hosts and power

Model `bandwidth` (dexvantage.core.studies.bandwidth): 3 of 3 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bandwidth.stated_mode_rates` | Stream data rate against the maker's stated rate for the mode | 0 | 0 | fraction | pass |
| `bandwidth.spec_figures` | USB capacities and bus-power allowances against the specifications | 0 | 1 × 10⁻¹² | relative | pass |
| `bandwidth.budget_recompute` | Bandwidth budget against an independent re-computation | 3.86 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | relative | pass |

- **`bandwidth.stated_mode_rates`** — Stream data rate against the maker's stated rate for the mode. *Compared:* how far the pixel payload (width × height × fps × bits per pixel) of the NanEyeC's 320 × 320 RAW10 mode exceeds the serial rate the maker states for it (0 when below; it must also be at least half of it). *Reference:* ams OSRAM NanEyeC datasheet: 75 Mbps at 58 Hz (SEIM), 63 Mbps at 49 Hz (LVDS) ([naneyec](#ref-naneyec)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The stated rates are the interface's serial bit rates, which carry the line and frame framing as well as the pixels: the pixel payload must not exceed them (tolerance 0) and the implied framing share, 25.6 to 26.3 %, is reported, not judged. It disagrees with the study's default overhead (5 %): the study's on-the-wire figure for these modes is up to 16.9 % below the stated serial rate. The default is meant for what a USB or GMSL link adds on top of the pixels, not for this sensor's own serial framing; for a link that carries the NanEyeC's raw serial stream, enter the stated rate as a measured figure or an overhead of about this share. No other maker in the library states a data rate for a stream mode, so no USB or GMSL device can be checked this way.
- **`bandwidth.spec_figures`** — USB capacities and bus-power allowances against the specifications. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the study's derived capacities (USB 2.0 bulk, USB 3.2 Gen 1, Gen 2, Gen 2x2) and bus-power allowances (USB 2.0, USB 3 one and two lanes) and the figures the specifications state elsewhere. *Reference:* USB 2.0 Table 5-10 and Table 3-1 of USB 3.2; USB 3.2 §4.4.11 ([usb20_spec](#ref-usb20_spec), [usb32_spec](#ref-usb32_spec)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Each figure is derived in the study from other statements of the same specification (unit loads and their count, transactions per microframe); the tolerance is rounding only.
- **`bandwidth.budget_recompute`** — Bandwidth budget against an independent re-computation. *Compared:* largest relative difference over seeded random topologies between the study and the re-computation: each sensor's rate on the wire and link load, each controller's load, each bus-powered device's current and port allowance, each bus-powered hub's draw, and the recording per episode and per campaign. *Reference:* the budget written out again in the check from the library's JSON files (its own stream lookup, hub walk, device generations and USB rules) ([usb20_spec](#ref-usb20_spec), [usb32_spec](#ref-usb32_spec)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both paths do the same arithmetic in a different order on the same stated figures, so they agree to rounding (1e-9 relative leaves room for summation order); a wrong stream lookup, a hub counted on the wrong controller or a wrong allowance shows as a whole-number factor.

### Brackets and mounts

Model `brackets` (dexvantage.core.studies.brackets): 3 of 3 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `brackets.watertight` | Bracket meshes are closed, manifold and outward | 0 | 0 | defects | pass |
| `brackets.volume` | Flange adapter disc volume and topology | 0.001801 | 0.01 | relative | pass |
| `brackets.iso_holes` | Flange adapter holes on the ISO 9409-1 pattern | 4.18 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.05 | mm | pass |

- **`brackets.watertight`** — Bracket meshes are closed, manifold and outward. *Compared:* defects over one bracket of each kind: edges not in exactly two triangles, directed edges used twice (inconsistent orientation), zero-area triangles, an Euler characteristic V - E + F that is odd or above 2 per shell, a signed volume that is not positive. *Reference:* the definitions of a closed orientable 2-manifold and of the divergence-theorem volume, written out in the check (independent of meshing.check) ([treece1999](#ref-treece1999), [euler_poincare](#ref-euler_poincare)).
  *Tolerance and why:* A printable STL must be a closed, consistently wound surface; any defect is a fault (a slicer may then fill or drop regions), so the tolerance is zero.
- **`brackets.volume`** — Flange adapter disc volume and topology. *Compared:* relative difference between the mesh volume of the ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 adapter disc (meshed at 0.25 mm, no fillets) and its closed-form volume; its Euler characteristic must equal 2 - 2g with g = 6 through holes. *Reference:* the volume of the disc written out from its cylinders: π t (R² - rc² - 4 rb² - rp²) + π h (rs² - rc²) - π h (rr² - rc²), and the Euler-Poincaré formula ([euler_poincare](#ref-euler_poincare), [ur5e_flange](#ref-ur5e_flange)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The mesher interpolates the distance linearly between grid points, so every sharp edge is cut by a fraction of a grid step; summed over the disc's edges that removes about 0.1 to 0.2 % of the volume (measured at 0.35 and 0.25 mm). 1 % allows for it while a wrong hole size (0.4 mm on a bolt hole is 1.5 % of its area) or a missing feature fails.
- **`brackets.iso_holes`** — Flange adapter holes on the ISO 9409-1 pattern. *Compared:* largest distance between a hole centre measured on the generated adapter's mesh (a circle fitted to the hole wall at mid-thickness) and its position in the ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 pattern; diameters must match the nominal plus the clearance within 0.1 mm. *Reference:* the pattern typed again in the check from Universal Robots' UR5e flange drawing and ISO 9409-1 Figure 1: bolt circle 50 mm, bolts at 45° + k 90°, the dowel on +x on the circle ([ur5e_flange](#ref-ur5e_flange), [iso9409_1](#ref-iso9409_1)).
  *Tolerance and why:* UR's drawing holds the bolt circle to ±0.1 mm on its diameter (±0.05 mm on a hole's radius position); a generated hole must sit well inside that, so 0.05 mm. A circle fitted to some hundred wall vertices locates its centre far better than the 0.25 mm grid.

- **`lighting.ggx_normalised`** — GGX normal distribution integrates to one (projected area). *Compared:* largest |∫ D(h) cos θ_h dω_h − 1| over α = 0.02 … 0.9. *Reference:* adaptive quadrature over θ_h (scipy.integrate.quad), D written out from Walter et al. 2007 eq. 33 ([walter2007](#ref-walter2007), [scipy_quad](#ref-scipy_quad)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Quadrature to 1e-12; the integral is exactly 1 for the GGX distribution, so 1e-6 leaves room only for the quadrature itself.
- **`lighting.white_furnace`** — Weak white furnace of the GGX microfacet BRDF (F = 1, G1 of the view). *Compared:* largest |∫ G1(ωo) D / (4 |n·ωo|) dωi − 1| over α = 0.02 … 0.9 and θo = 0 … 89°, by adaptive quadrature; the Monte Carlo estimate with h ~ D cos θ_h must also lie within four standard errors of 1. *Reference:* the exact value 1 (Heitz 2014, the weak white furnace test): scipy.integrate.quad over θ_h with the φ integral in closed form ([heitz2014](#ref-heitz2014), [walter2007](#ref-walter2007), [scipy_quad](#ref-scipy_quad)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The measured figure is the quadrature (exact to about 10⁻⁹). The Monte Carlo estimator, shown in the figure, grows as 1 / cos θo at grazing view on rough surfaces, so its standard error is largest at 89° and α 0.9; it must lie within four standard errors of 1.
- **`lighting.energy`** — Energy conservation of every material's BRDF (directional albedo ≤ 1). *Compared:* how far the largest directional albedo ∫ f_r cos θ_i dωi, less three standard errors, exceeds 1, over the material tags and θo = 0 … 89°. *Reference:* the bound 1 (a passive surface reflects no more than arrives), Monte Carlo with multiple importance sampling ([veach1997](#ref-veach1997), [walter2007](#ref-walter2007), [ashikhmin2000](#ref-ashikhmin2000)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The tolerance is 0: any albedo above 1 by more than three standard errors fails.
- **`lighting.reciprocity`** — Helmholtz reciprocity of the BRDF. *Compared:* largest |f_r(ωi, ωo) − f_r(ωo, ωi)| / max f_r over 20 000 random pairs per material tag. *Reference:* the identity f_r(ωi, ωo) = f_r(ωo, ωi) (Helmholtz reciprocity) ([walter2007](#ref-walter2007), [ashikhmin2000](#ref-ashikhmin2000)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both terms are symmetric by construction; the tolerance allows rounding only.
- **`lighting.peak_closed_form`** — Specular peak at normal incidence against its closed form. *Compared:* largest relative difference between f_r(n, n) and F0 / (4π α²) + (28 ρ / 23π)(1 − F0)(1 − 2⁻⁵)², over the material tags and α = 0.02 … 0.9. *Reference:* the closed form written out again, F0 from the index by ((n − 1)² + k²) / ((n + 1)² + k²) ([walter2007](#ref-walter2007), [schlick1994](#ref-schlick1994), [ashikhmin2000](#ref-ashikhmin2000), [hecht2017](#ref-hecht2017)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Exact arithmetic but for rounding (the GGX D at cos θ_h = 1 is 1 / (π α²)).
- **`lighting.schlick_vs_fresnel`** — Schlick's Fresnel against the exact Fresnel equations. *Compared:* largest |F_Schlick(θ) − (R_s + R_p) / 2| over θ = 0 … 90° for the dielectrics (PMMA, BK7); aluminium reported. *Reference:* the Fresnel equations for a smooth interface (Hecht, Optics, §4.6.2), complex index ([schlick1994](#ref-schlick1994), [hecht2017](#ref-hecht2017), [sultanova2009](#ref-sultanova2009), [schott_bk7](#ref-schott_bk7), [mcpeak2015](#ref-mcpeak2015)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Schlick's approximation is exact at 0° and 90° and largest in between near grazing; for n ≈ 1.5 it stays below 0.04 (measured here), which the tolerance states. For aluminium the difference reaches 0.080, a known limit of the model (docs).
- **`lighting.inverse_square`** — Point-light inverse-square law against Monte Carlo over an area light. *Compared:* relative difference between I / d² (I = L a²) and the Monte Carlo irradiance of a Lambertian square of side a, on its axis, at d ≥ 10 a (largest). *Reference:* Monte Carlo integration of ∫ L cos θ_e cos θ_r / r² dA over the square ([mcluney2014](#ref-mcluney2014)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The point law is the far-field limit: expanding the closed form of the square, its relative error is about (a / d)² / 3, 1.3 % at d = 5 a and 0.33 % at d = 10 a, so 0.5 % from ten source sizes on states it; the Monte Carlo error at this sample count is below 10⁻⁴.
- **`lighting.area_vs_closed_form`** — Area light split into patches against the closed form. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the 4 × 4-patch area light (core/lights) and the closed-form irradiance of a 0.6 m square panel, receivers 0.3–2 m away and up to 0.5 m off its axis; and the closed form against Monte Carlo. *Reference:* the configuration factor of a rectangle to a parallel element at its corner, summed over four corner rectangles (Howell's catalogue), and Monte Carlo ([howell_catalog](#ref-howell_catalog), [mcluney2014](#ref-mcluney2014)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The split converges as 1 / n² (patches per side n); with the default 4 × 4 the largest difference is about 2 % at half the panel's size, where the patch is a quarter of the distance; 2.5 % states that bound.
- **`lighting.visibility_vs_raycast`** — The study's camera and light visibility against exact ray casting. *Compared:* share of the sampled object, gripper and table area (area-weighted) where the study's visibility (cube maps with its slope-scaled tolerance) disagrees with exact ray casting, over every camera and light at the working poses of the UR5e sample with a can, a Key Light and a window. *Reference:* core/raycast first hits along each line of sight against the full posed scene (no cube map), to the same lifted points ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [williams1978](#ref-williams1978)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The disagreements are within about a texel of a silhouette or a contact (the cube map is sampled per texel; at 512 texels one spans 3.9 mrad at a face centre) and where the slope tolerance lets a point just behind an oblique edge through. Measured on the RTX 5080: 0.66 % of the area at 512 texels, 0.85 % at 256, 0.31 % at 1024.
