- **`dexhand.blind_gap_bruteforce`** — Sensory blind gap against a brute-force scan of the approach. *Compared:* largest difference between the blind gap (coarse distances, refined inside transitions) and a scan of every distance at the refine spacing, over the fingertips of one approach on the dexhand sample with a wall. *Reference:* brute-force scan of the approach with the same visibility kernel ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997)).
  *Tolerance and why:* 13 visibility evaluations against 21 for the scan; the tolerance is one refine step.
- **`dexhand.matrix_vs_analytic`** — Finger × camera occlusion matrix against a closed form. *Compared:* largest difference between the study's share of a pad hidden by each owner (or seen) and the closed form, over the 2 pads × 2 cameras × owners of a scripted two-finger scene with a palm plate; the default (ray-cast) path and the cube-map path at n = 2048. *Reference:* central projection of a box finger's top face onto the other finger's pad plane, and of a palm plate's edge seen from a low side camera, written out in the check (point counts on a 20 × 20 grid) ([hartley2004](#ref-hartley2004), [moller1997](#ref-moller1997)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Every pad point lies 0.5 mm (on the pad plane) from a shadow edge, which is 1.7 mrad from camera 1 and more from camera 2, against a texel of 1 mrad at n = 2048: no point is ambiguous for either path, so both must reproduce the closed form point for point. 1e-3 (less than one of the 400 points of a pad) allows nothing else.
- **`dexhand.owner_vs_bruteforce`** — Owner of the first hit against an all-pairs ray cast. *Compared:* fraction of patch points whose first-hit owner (or "seen") from the study's default kernel differs from an all-pairs Möller–Trumbore cast that keeps the nearest triangle; random two-finger and palm box scenes, random camera positions. *Reference:* Möller–Trumbore ray–triangle intersection against every triangle, nearest hit kept by index, written out in the check (no grid; no code shared with core/raycast.py) ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both are exact ray–triangle tests; they can differ only for a ray through a shared edge or corner (rounding) or a hit within rounding of the 1 mm visibility margin. 1e-3 leaves room for those and nothing else. The scenes must show at least three owners (seen, its own finger and another group) for the check to count.
- **`dexhand.cube_owner_union`** — Owner-group cube maps against one cube map of the scene. *Compared:* largest difference (m) between min over the owner groups' cube-map distances and one cube map of the whole scene, along random directions; dexhand sample, power grasp, every camera. *Reference:* core/occlusion.py CubeMap of the whole scene (a z-buffer of the union of the groups) ([greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The cube map of a union keeps, per texel, the nearest of the triangles drawn into it, so the minimum over maps of disjoint groups must equal it exactly (float32 distances on the GPU, the same arithmetic per group); 1e-6 m allows float32 rounding of a distance near 1 m. The detail lists, per camera and finger, how many points (percent of the patch) the cube-map path sees differently from exact ray casting at this face size: the texel effect that makes ray casting the study's default.

- **`cables.routed_arc`** — Routed cable length over a revolute joint. *Compared:* largest difference between the study's routed length (swept over the hinge's range, robot base moved and rotated) and the closed form, in three cases: the circle arc (equal radii, dz = 0), the helix (dz = 40 mm) and unequal radii over a smaller wrap radius; the unwrapped angle must equal the geometric angle modulo 2π. *Reference:* the circle arc r·|q − α₀|, the helix √((r·|q − α₀|)² + dz²) and the belt-over-a-pulley length, written out in the check ([docarmo1976](#ref-docarmo1976)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both sides compute the same closed form in float64 from link poses MuJoCo gives (with the base pose applied), so they agree to rounding, about 1e-16 m; 1e-9 m leaves room for that while a wrong side sign, a wrong home angle or a length reduced to a half turn shows as centimetres.
- **`cables.helix_bend`** — Bend radius of a taut run on the joint cylinder. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the helix's radius of curvature and, for a taut run wrapped on the cylinder, both the study's bend radius estimate and the drawn 49-point polyline's (the smallest circle through three consecutive points), over the hinge's range where the run wraps more than 0.5 rad. *Reference:* the helix's curvature a / c² (radius c² / a, a = r, c² = r² + b², b = dz / θ) [do Carmo 1976] ([docarmo1976](#ref-docarmo1976)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The estimate is the circle through three consecutive polyline points; on a helix that circle differs from the osculating one by a share of order (Δφ)² of the angle step Δφ between points (here up to 0.1 rad), a few parts in ten thousand; 0.5 % bounds that.
- **`cables.loop_arc`** — Slack loop on a straight run against the circular arc. *Compared:* largest relative difference between the radius of the circular arc of length s over c and both the study's slack-loop radius estimate and the drawn 49-point loop polyline's (laid length s over a straight run of chord c), for 200 random (c, s) with s / c from 1.02 to 6. *Reference:* R = s / (2β), sin β / β = c / s, β found with scipy.optimize.brentq ([scipy_brentq](#ref-scipy_brentq)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The loop's points lie on the circle, so the three-point circle is the arc itself; what remains is the polyline being slightly shorter than the arc it samples (the bisection matches the polyline's length to s), well under 0.5 % at 49 points.
- **`cables.snag_bruteforce`** — Snag detection against brute-force sampling. *Compared:* poses (of the hinge's trajectory over its range, the robot base moved and rotated, a slack loop laid with room to swing into two posts) where the study's snag flag differs from brute force, grazing poses (the deepest point within 1 mm of a surface) left out; the share of time snagged at the study's 2° sampling must be within two steps of brute force at 0.2°. *Reference:* the loop resampled every 0.5 mm, each point tested against every box in its own frame in closed form ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both sides test the same loop polylines; the study by ray casting segments against triangles and a parity test, brute force by points 0.5 mm apart in closed-form boxes. A loop that only grazes a box (less than 1 mm deep or clear) can fall between the brute-force points, so those poses are not counted; every other pose must agree. Between the sampled poses the swept volume is not tested: the share-of-time comparison shows how much that sampling misses.

- **`formats.tfrecord_crc`** — TFRecord CRC-32C. *Compared:* CRC-32C values that differ from the published vectors or from a bit-at-a-time reference, masked CRCs that differ from TensorFlow's formula, and TFRecord framing read wrongly or damage not refused. *Reference:* RFC 3720 appendix B.4 test vectors and the CRC catalogue check value of CRC-32/ISCSI; a bitwise Castagnoli CRC and the TFRecord framing written again in the check ([rfc3720](#ref-rfc3720), [crc_catalogue](#ref-crc_catalogue), [tfrecord_format](#ref-tfrecord_format)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Zero: a checksum is exact; one wrong bit would accept damaged records or refuse good ones.
- **`formats.mjcf_scene`** — MuJoCo scene file loads in MuJoCo and poses like the project. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between each scene camera's optical centre in the saved MJCF, loaded from disk by mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path and posed at a random joint state set by joint name, and the same camera posed by DexVantage's kinematics; also every camera's rotation within 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad and intrinsics within 10⁻² px; the UR5e, SO-100 and dexhand samples. *Reference:* core/camrender.optical_pose (RobotModel forward kinematics of the stored robot files, the mount and the imager pose) and the imagers' lens models; MuJoCo's XML parser reading the written files ([mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317), [mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The file is the one Simulate ▸ Build the MuJoCo scene… writes, read back by MuJoCo from disk with its assets folder, so a missing mesh, a wrong path or a pose lost in writing shows here. MuJoCo 3.17.0's XML writer (MjSpec.to_xml, no precision option) writes 6 significant digits: half a unit of the 6th digit is 5 × 10⁻⁷ m on a coordinate under 1 m, about 10⁻⁶ rad on a quaternion and 0.005 px on a focal length of 1 000 to 9 999 px (focalpixel "1396.81"). The tolerances, 2 µm, 5 × 10⁻⁶ rad and 0.01 px, allow that rounding along a few links of a chain (measured 2026-11-07: 5.8 × 10⁻⁷ m, 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ rad, 1.9 × 10⁻³ px); a pose wrong by a link offset is millimetres. In memory, before writing, the scene matches within 10⁻⁴ px (groundtruth.scene_intrinsics).
- **`formats.mjcf_snippets`** — MJCF camera snippets load in MuJoCo and pose like the project. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between each camera of the exported <camera>/<site> snippets, pasted into its body of the robot's own MJCF and loaded by MuJoCo, posed at a random joint state by joint name, and the same camera posed by DexVantage; also every rotation within 10⁻⁹ rad and the intrinsics MuJoCo compiles within 10⁻³ px; the UR5e, SO-100 and dexhand samples. *Reference:* core/camrender.optical_pose (RobotModel forward kinematics, the mount and the imager pose) and the imagers' lens models; MuJoCo's XML parser reading the snippets ([mujoco_camera_317](#ref-mujoco_camera_317), [mujoco_xml](#ref-mujoco_xml)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The snippets are written with 17 significant digits (they read back to the same float64), so the poses agree to rounding (10⁻⁹ m and rad leave room for a chain of a dozen bodies); MuJoCo stores the compiled intrinsics in float32 (about 6 × 10⁻⁵ px at a 1 000 px focal length), hence 10⁻³ px. The pasted file is also loaded through MuJoCo's own writer to show every camera is found under its body; the figures come from each block parsed by MuJoCo and attached to the robot's model in memory, since that writer keeps 6 digits. The full scene is formats.mjcf_scene.
- **`formats.urdf_roundtrip`** — URDF parses and its sensor frames match DexVantage's kinematics. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between every sensor body frame and optical frame of the exported rig.urdf, posed at a random joint state (1) by a forward-kinematics walk of the XML with urdfdom's origin and RPY rules and (2) by MuJoCo's URDF compiler, and the same frames from DexVantage; also every rotation within 10⁻⁹ rad and no structural problem (one root, every link reached once, complete <limit> elements); the three samples. *Reference:* scenegeom.sensor_world_pose and camrender.optical_pose; Python's ElementTree with urdfdom's setFromRPY quaternion and Rodrigues' rotation written again; MuJoCo's URDF compiler ([urdfdom](#ref-urdfdom), [urdf](#ref-urdf), [mujoco_urdf](#ref-mujoco_urdf), [python_ast](#ref-python_ast)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The URDF is written from the MuJoCo model DexVantage compiles, joint by joint (anchors and qpos0 folded into the origins), with 17 significant digits; two independent posers, an XML walk with urdfdom's conventions and MuJoCo's URDF compiler, must both agree with DexVantage to rounding (10⁻⁹ m over chains of up to 30 joints). A wrong joint anchor, a sign of qpos0 or an RPY order would be millimetres or degrees.
- **`formats.ros2_tf`** — Static transform launch file and tf2 tree pose the cameras like DexVantage. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between each optical frame posed from the exported static_transforms.launch.py (its static_transform_publisher arguments read with Python's ast) on its parent link at a random joint state, or from tf_tree.yaml's world pose at the export's joint state (PyYAML), and the frame posed by DexVantage; rotations within 10⁻⁹ rad; the launch file and the tree list the same frames; the three samples. *Reference:* camrender.optical_pose; RobotModel.link_pose for the parent link; tf2_ros's argument names ([tf2_static_publisher](#ref-tf2_static_publisher), [pyyaml](#ref-pyyaml), [python_ast](#ref-python_ast), [rep103](#ref-rep103)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The transforms are numbers written with 17 significant digits: any error beyond rounding is a wrong frame, parent or quaternion order (tf2 takes x, y, z, w).
- **`formats.opencv_yaml`** — OpenCV YAML read back by cv2.FileStorage equals the source. *Compared:* largest absolute difference between what cv2.FileStorage reads back from each imager's YAML (image size, K, the 4 × 4 extrinsics) and cameras.json and the source; and every lens projected through cv2.projectPoints or cv2.fisheye.projectPoints with the written K and D within 10⁻⁶ px of DexVantage's lens model when the mapping is exact, within the stated error when it is an approximation; seven lens models on the UR5e sample's six imagers. *Reference:* the source CameraModel and transforms; OpenCV's own projection functions ([opencv_filestorage](#ref-opencv_filestorage), [opencv_calib3d](#ref-opencv_calib3d), [opencv_fisheye](#ref-opencv_fisheye)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Zero: cv2.FileStorage writes doubles with 17 significant digits, so a matrix reads back bit for bit (measured 0 on 2026-11-07). The projection bound of 10⁻⁶ px is far above float64 rounding (10⁻¹² px measured) and far below any wrong coefficient order; the equisolid and stereographic lenses have no OpenCV form and must stay within the error the file states (measured 5 × 10⁻⁹ and 4 × 10⁻⁴ px on these lenses).
- **`formats.kalibr_camchain`** — Kalibr camchain parsed back equals the rig. *Compared:* largest absolute difference between camchain.yaml read with PyYAML (intrinsics [fu fv pu pv], exact distortion terms, T_cn_cnm1) and the chain from DexVantage's optical poses, inv(T_world_cn) · T_world_cnm1; also Kalibr's keys, model names and coefficient counts (ConfigReader); seven lens models on the UR5e sample and the sample itself. *Reference:* camrender.optical_pose and the lens models; Kalibr's ConfigReader rules ([kalibr_yaml](#ref-kalibr_yaml), [pyyaml](#ref-pyyaml)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Zero: the numbers are written in Python's shortest round-trip form, which YAML reads back to the same float64.
- **`formats.masks_vs_occlusion`** — Exported masks match the occlusion study per pixel. *Compared:* share of sampled pixels (every 4th row and column; 8th in a quick run) where the exported self-occlusion PNG differs from exact ray casting against the occlusion study's occluders (robot hit nearer than any other); also within 0.5 % of the occlusion study's cube map (n = 2048) and the depth-validity codes within 1 % of the conditions evaluated again per pixel by exact ray casting; the UR5e sample's two cameras and two depth sensors. *Reference:* core/raycast.py (Möller-Trumbore on a uniform grid) on scenegeom.sensor_occluders; core/occlusion.CubeMap; the depth-validity conditions written again ([moller1997](#ref-moller1997), [amanatides_woo1987](#ref-amanatides_woo1987), [greene1986](#ref-greene1986)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The masks come from the Camera view's renderer, which tests each pixel-centre ray against every triangle exactly, so exact ray casting should agree but for rays through a shared edge (10⁻³; measured 0 of 187 200 pixels on 2026-11-07). The cube map answers per texel (0.03° at 2048), so silhouettes may differ by a texel: 0.5 % (measured 0.07 %). The depth codes use the study's cube maps for the other imager's line of sight: 1 % (measured 0.25 %, at silhouettes; at the study's own 512 texels it was 4.4 %, the reason the masks use 2048).
- **`formats.bracket_step`** — Bracket STEP read back by OpenCASCADE equals its mesh. *Compared:* relative difference between the volume of the exported bracket STEP, read back by gmsh's OpenCASCADE kernel, and the volume of the faceted mesh it was written from (divergence theorem); also exactly one volume and the bounding box within 10⁻³ mm; the UR5e sample's wrist bracket at a 2 mm grid. *Reference:* the triangle mesh (core/meshing.py) by the divergence theorem; OpenCASCADE's own STEP reader and mass properties ([step_ap](#ref-step_ap), [gmsh](#ref-gmsh)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The STEP is the mesh itself (each triangle a planar face, sewn into one shell), so the volumes agree to the STEP file's number format and OpenCASCADE's sewing tolerance; 10⁻⁶ of the volume is far below a missing or flipped face (a face of a 2 mm grid is about 10⁻⁴ of a bracket). Registered only when gmsh is installed.
- **`formats.isaac_usd`** — Isaac USD camera prims re-opened match the cameras. *Compared:* largest pixel gap between points projected through each exported camera prim (pxr's Gf.Camera frustum of the prim as re-opened, files written by pxr and by the text writer) and through the imager's pinhole part; also every prim's world transform within 10⁻⁹ m and 10⁻⁶ rad, focal length and apertures within 10⁻⁶ relative, and its OpenCV lens attributes; the three samples, two of their cameras given a Brown-Conrady and a Kannala-Brandt unit calibration. *Reference:* core/camrender.optical_pose and the imagers' lens models (optics.CameraModel); OpenUSD's own camera model (pxr UsdGeom.Camera, Gf.Camera) ([openusd_camera](#ref-openusd_camera), [isaaclab_camera_v300](#ref-isaaclab_camera_v300)).
  *Tolerance and why:* USD stores focalLength, the apertures and the OpenCV attributes as 32-bit floats (a relative error up to 6 × 10⁻⁸, so about 10⁻⁴ px at a 1 400 px focal length across a 1 920 px image); 10⁻³ px allows that with margin and is far below a sign or convention error (an aperture offset of the wrong sign moves the principal point by twice its offset, tens of pixels on the calibrated cameras here). Measured 2026-11-07: 2.6 × 10⁻⁵ px. Transforms are matrix4d (64-bit): 10⁻⁹ m and 10⁻⁶ rad are far below a frame-convention error (a quarter or half turn), measured 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ m and 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁶ rad.
- **`formats.isaac_config`** — Isaac Lab camera configs compile and their values match. *Compared:* largest position difference (m) between each camera's CameraCfg offset in the generated Isaac Lab v3.0.0 and v2.3.2 Python files (parsed with ast, executed against stub classes with the fields of the cited source) and the camera's pose in its parent frame; also orientation within 10⁻⁹ rad in each release's quaternion order, focal length and OpenCV intrinsics within 10⁻⁹ relative, the randomisation bounds equal to core/tolerance.bounds, perturbed_offset within 10⁻⁹ m and 10⁻⁹ rad of the same draw applied by core/tolerance.apply_draw, and sample_offset within the bounds; the three samples with calibrated lenses. *Reference:* core/camrender.optical_pose taken to the parent link by RobotModel.link_pose; core/tolerance and core/factors for the draws; the Isaac Lab v3.0.0 and v2.3.2 source for the field names ([isaaclab_camera_v300](#ref-isaaclab_camera_v300), [isaaclab_camera_v232](#ref-isaaclab_camera_v232)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The files write every number with 17 significant digits (Python's repr), so values read back to the last bit and the differences are the rounding of composing the transforms in another order (measured 2026-11-07: 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ m, 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ rad); 10⁻⁹ m and rad is far below a mount or quaternion-order error (millimetres, degrees). Isaac Lab itself is not installed here: the stub classes refuse any field the v3.0.0 or v2.3.2 source does not define and require the ones it leaves MISSING.
- **`formats.lerobot_export`** — LeRobot info.json and train configs agree with the reader and the source. *Compared:* mismatches: the exported v2.1 and v3.0 info.json against the info.json of a dataset written with the same features (state names, camera keys and sizes) and read back by DexVantage's LeRobot reader (keys, dtypes, shapes, names, video sizes and rates, paths); train-config keys that are not fields of the pinned TrainPipelineConfig, DatasetConfig or policy config; feature types; ACT's temporal-ensembling rule; camera shapes against info.json; the ACT and Diffusion Policy YAML through PyYAML and the OpenVLA entry executed against stub enums; the UR5e sample with its action-chunk recommendation applied. *Reference:* core/datasets/lerobot (write_lerobot and LeRobotDataset); the LeRobot source at commit d490e47 (field names); ACT, Diffusion Policy and OpenVLA sources at their pinned commits ([lerobot_dataset_format](#ref-lerobot_dataset_format), [lerobot_train_config](#ref-lerobot_train_config), [act_repo](#ref-act_repo), [diffusion_policy_repo](#ref-diffusion_policy_repo), [openvla_oxe](#ref-openvla_oxe)).
  *Tolerance and why:* LeRobot, ACT, Diffusion Policy and OpenVLA are not installed here, so their own loaders are not run: info.json is checked through DexVantage's reader (itself checked against the format by formats.lerobot_roundtrip), and the configs against the field names of the pinned sources. The codec fields are not compared (the writer uses H.264 where PyAV has no AV1 encoder).
- **`formats.report`** — Report HTML parses and lists every study present. *Compared:* mismatches when report.html, built over five studies of the UR5e sample with requirements on two of them, is parsed by Python's html.parser: a study result without its section and heading, a section without a result, a study neither reported nor listed as not run, no scorecard, no provenance block with the project's content hash, fewer figures than the sections that have one; and report.pdf without a study or the hash when read by pdftotext (poppler), where installed. *Reference:* the report's own results document (report.json) and core.provenance.project_digest; Python's html.parser; poppler's pdftotext ([html_living_standard](#ref-html_living_standard), [pdf_32000](#ref-pdf_32000), [poppler_pdftotext](#ref-poppler_pdftotext)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Studies that refuse on this project are listed under "Not run" with their sentence, which the check accepts.
- **`formats.rerun_rrd_readback`** — Rerun .rrd file read back by Rerun's own reader. *Compared:* largest difference between what the bridge logged and what rerun.chunk.RrdReader reads back: every camera's Pinhole intrinsics and resolution (px), its imager transform (m) and the gripper link's transform at one time of the UR5e sample's trajectory against forward kinematics (m); every entity path present and the audit flags on the episode timeline. *Reference:* rerun-sdk's own .rrd reader; the library's lens figures; MuJoCo forward kinematics ([rerun_sdk](#ref-rerun_sdk), [mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012)).
- **`formats.canonical_warp_files`** — Canonical warp export read back. *Compared:* largest difference between the arrays and numbers written and those read back: the .yml maps through cv2.FileStorage against the .npy maps, the grid_sample grid against (2u + 1)/W − 1 of the maps, the JSON homography against the model's, the canonical view file loaded back. *Reference:* OpenCV's FileStorage reader, numpy.load, json and the grid formula written out here ([opencv_filestorage](#ref-opencv_filestorage)).

- **`samples.aloha_cameras`** — ALOHA 2: the four cameras against the model's cameras. *Compared:* largest difference between each ALOHA 2 sensor's world pose (DexVantage forward kinematics and mount) and the MuJoCo camera it is read from (positions in m and rotation-matrix entries), at random joint values. *Reference:* MuJoCo's camera frames (mj_camlight) of aloha.xml (wrist_cam_left, wrist_cam_right) and scene_parts.xml (overhead_cam, worms_eye_cam, copied from scene.xml) ([aloha2_2024](#ref-aloha2_2024), [menagerie_98a70c5](#ref-menagerie_98a70c5), [mujoco_camera](#ref-mujoco_camera)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The wrist cameras ride on the arm files (to_xml rounding, as for the arms); the two frame cameras are read from scene_parts.xml through aloha.xml's base pose. 1e-6 allows the rounding only.
- **`samples.g1_held_legs`** — G1: the upper body against the full model at "stand". *Compared:* largest difference of any link pose (position in m, rotation-matrix entries) of the G1 upper-body robot (free joint, legs and waist deleted) from the same body of g1_with_hands.xml at "stand" with the same arm and hand values. *Reference:* MuJoCo Menagerie g1_with_hands.xml (as bundled, meshes simplified) compiled and posed by MuJoCo directly, its free joint, legs and waist at the "stand" keyframe ([menagerie_98a70c5](#ref-menagerie_98a70c5), [mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The upper-body file deletes joints that are 0 at "stand", so their bodies stay where the keyframe puts them; what remains is MuJoCo's to_xml rounding (1e-6).
- **`samples.g1_head_camera`** — G1: the head camera against Unitree's URDF. *Compared:* largest difference between the G1 head camera's world pose (DexVantage) and Unitree's d435_joint origin composed on torso_link (positions in m and rotation-matrix entries). *Reference:* Unitree's g1_29dof_rev_1_0.urdf joint d435_joint (xyz, rpy as URDF writes them: R = Rz Ry Rx) on the torso_link pose of g1_with_hands.xml posed by MuJoCo at "stand" ([unitree_g1_urdf](#ref-unitree_g1_urdf), [menagerie_98a70c5](#ref-menagerie_98a70c5)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Both sides compose the same figures by different routes (a quaternion through the mount against the URDF's rotation written out here); only floating-point rounding remains.
- **`samples.panda_instances`** — Bimanual Panda: both instances against panda.xml. *Compared:* largest difference of any link pose (position in m, rotation-matrix entries) of the two Panda robots from panda.xml's bodies at the same joint values, moved by each robot's base pose. *Reference:* MuJoCo Menagerie franka_emika_panda/panda.xml (as bundled: OBJ meshes as STL, bodies unchanged) compiled and posed by MuJoCo directly ([menagerie_98a70c5](#ref-menagerie_98a70c5), [mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The file's bodies are not rewritten (only its mesh file names), so only the base pose's floating-point composition remains; 1e-9 m is far below any figure the studies report.

Model `workspace` (dexvantage.core.workspace_check): 2 of 2 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |

- **`workspace.object_extent`** — Workspace: the bounding box of a turned object against closed forms. *Compared:* largest shortfall or overshoot of an object's world bounding box (from its triangles) against the true shape's, as a share of the bound the tessellation allows (0 for a box, r (1 − cos²(π/24)) for a cylinder or a sphere). *Reference:* the box of a turned box |R| h (Arvo 1990); of a cylinder r sqrt(1 − a_i²) + (h/2)|a_i|; of a sphere r (written out here); rotations from SciPy ([arvo1990](#ref-arvo1990), [scipy_rotation](#ref-scipy_rotation)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The tessellated cylinder and sphere lie inside the true shapes, so their boxes may fall short by up to 1.70 % of the radius and never stick out; a box is exact to rounding. A wrong rotation or a size read as a diameter shows as many times the bound.
- **`workspace.inside_classification`** — Workspace: objects inside or outside task volumes. *Compared:* objects classified inside or outside every task volume differently from the exact classification of the true shape's box (objects at least 3 mm from every face). *Reference:* exact boxes of the true shapes (closed forms above) against the volumes' boxes ([arvo1990](#ref-arvo1990)).
  *Tolerance and why:* Every object is clear of each face by 3 mm (more than the 1 mm tolerance plus the 1.7 % tessellation shortfall of a 60 mm radius), so the classification is unambiguous: any disagreement is a fault.

- **`robot_io.urdf_mujoco`** — Exported URDF loads in MuJoCo as written, with the robots' inertials. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between every sensor body and optical frame of the exported rig.urdf, loaded unchanged by mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_path and posed by mj_kinematics at 10 random joint states, and the same frame from DexVantage; also every rotation within 10⁻⁶ rad, the file loads, and each robot body's mass and inertia tensor within 10⁻⁹ (relative) and centre of mass within 10⁻⁹ m of the robot's own MuJoCo model; the SO-100, UR5e and bimanual Panda samples. *Reference:* camrender.optical_pose and scenegeom.sensor_world_pose; MuJoCo's URDF compiler; the robots' MuJoCo models compiled from their own files (body_mass, body_ipos, body_iquat, body_inertia) ([mujoco_urdf](#ref-mujoco_urdf), [urdfdom](#ref-urdfdom), [urdf](#ref-urdf)).
  *Tolerance and why:* 10⁻⁶ m is the round trip's stated requirement; the file writes 17 significant digits, so the error is rounding (measured 2026-11-07: 5.3 × 10⁻¹⁶ m) and a wrong joint anchor or frame would be millimetres. Inertials: MuJoCo's URDF compiler diagonalises the written full tensor again, so 10⁻⁹ relative leaves room for its eigen-decomposition only. Before this export wrote inertials, MuJoCo refused the file ("mass and inertia of moving bodies must be larger than mjMINVAL").
- **`robot_io.usd_roundtrip`** — USD robot import: bundled robots written to USD and read back. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between every link of the SO-100, UR5e (with the 2F-85) and Panda samples and the same link of the robot written to a UsdPhysics articulation (core/robot/usd_writer.py) and imported back (core/robot/usd_import.py), over 50 random joint states; also every rotation within 10⁻⁶ rad, the joint limits equal to the float32 the file stores and within its spacing of the source, the writer's body poses as pxr composes them within 10⁻⁶ m, masses within 10⁻⁶ relative. *Reference:* the robots' MuJoCo models compiled from their own files (mj_kinematics); pxr's XformCache for the written stage ([openusd_physics](#ref-openusd_physics), [mujoco_menagerie](#ref-mujoco_menagerie)).
  *Tolerance and why:* UsdPhysics stores joint frames as point3f and quatf and limits as float (32-bit): about 6 × 10⁻⁸ relative, so a chain of a dozen joints within a metre lands within a few 10⁻⁸ m (measured 2026-11-07: 2.5 × 10⁻⁸ m, 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ rad); 10⁻⁶ m and rad leave that margin and sit far below a convention error (a sign of the axis, an anchor or a frame swap is millimetres or degrees). "Exact" limits: the imported limit equals the stored float32 decoded (degrees × π/180), which is within one float32 spacing of the source.
- **`robot_io.usd_third_party`** — USD robot import: a third party's UR5e against DexVantage's. *Compared:* largest distance (m) between the seven arm bodies of the newton-assets UR5e (a UsdPhysics articulation written by the mujoco-usd-converter from Menagerie's ur5e.xml), imported by DexVantage, and the same bodies of DexVantage's UR5e sample over 50 random arm states; also rotations within 10⁻⁶ rad, the six joint limits within 10⁻⁶ rad and the arm masses within 10⁻⁶ relative. *Reference:* Menagerie's ur5e.xml compiled by MuJoCo (the UR5e sample); the third party's converter, not DexVantage's writer, made the file ([newton_assets_ur5e](#ref-newton_assets_ur5e), [openusd_physics](#ref-openusd_physics)).
  *Tolerance and why:* An independent writer: a sign, axis or frame convention the importer and DexVantage's writer shared by mistake would show here. The file stores float32 frames and limits (degrees), hence 10⁻⁶. Its mesh library (6.3 MB) is not bundled, so its visual meshes are left out and said; the bodies, joints, limits, masses and collision primitives are read. Measured 2026-11-07: 2.6 × 10⁻⁸ m, 1.9 × 10⁻¹⁵ rad.
- **`robot_io.openvla_encoding`** — OpenVLA export picks its encodings from the rig. *Compared:* number of mismatches over six rigs (SO-100 with joint and end-effector actions, UR5e, ALOHA 2 with and without an OpenVLA-OFT policy, the bimanual Panda) between the exported state and action encodings, whether they fit, the image keys and the notes, and the pinned sources' rules restated in the check; each written entry executed against OpenVLA's enum classes copied verbatim from configs.py L33-50. *Reference:* OpenVLA configs.py L33-50 and materialize.py L32-33 at c8f03f4; OpenVLA-OFT materialize.py L32-33, L43-45 and configs.py L681-687 at e4287e9 ([openvla_materialize](#ref-openvla_materialize), [openvla_oft](#ref-openvla_oft), [openvla_oxe](#ref-openvla_oxe)).
  *Tolerance and why:* The rules are a table of the sources' statements (which action encodings each loader accepts, the 7 + 1 and 2 × (6 + 1) layouts); a zero means every rig got the encoding those lines give and the export says when none fits. Not run in OpenVLA itself (not installed).
- **`robot_io.isaac_principal_point`** — Isaac export: an off-centre principal point reaches Isaac Lab. *Compared:* largest difference (px) between each camera's fx, fy, cx, cy and the intrinsics Isaac Lab v3.0.0 would build from the exported prim (its camera.py rule written again, applied to the prim as pxr re-opens it), two cameras given off-centre principal points (one a pinhole without distortion); also every off-centre camera named with its offset in the export notes, in the Export dialog's lines and as not representable at v2.3.2 in isaac_cameras.json. *Reference:* the imagers' lens models; Isaac Lab v3.0.0 camera.py L828-857, L879-904 and sensors.py L162-165 ([isaaclab_intrinsics](#ref-isaaclab_intrinsics), [isaaclab_camera_v300](#ref-isaaclab_camera_v300), [isaaclab_camera_v232](#ref-isaaclab_camera_v232), [openusd_camera](#ref-openusd_camera)).
  *Tolerance and why:* USD stores the OpenCV attributes as 32-bit floats (about 3 × 10⁻⁵ px at 640 px); 10⁻³ px leaves margin and is far below the effect checked: without the OpenCV attributes Isaac Lab centres the principal point (cx = width / 2), 16.6 and 28.5 px off on these cameras. Measured 2026-11-07: 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ px. Not rendered in Isaac Sim (not installed).

- **`stats.t_tests`** — Welch and paired t tests. *Compared:* largest difference of p, t and the interval ends over 20 random data sets. *Reference:* scipy.stats.ttest_ind(equal_var=False) and ttest_rel with confidence_interval() ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.rank_tests`** — Mann-Whitney U and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. *Compared:* largest p-value difference over exact, permutation and asymptotic cases and three alternatives. *Reference:* scipy.stats.mannwhitneyu and scipy.stats.wilcoxon (method auto) ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.fisher_odds`** — Fisher's exact test and the odds ratio interval. *Compared:* largest difference of p and of the Woolf interval ends over eight 2 × 2 tables. *Reference:* scipy.stats.fisher_exact and scipy.stats.contingency.odds_ratio(kind="sample") ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.permutation_exact`** — Exact permutation tests. *Compared:* largest p-value difference over unpaired (every relabelling) and paired (every sign flip) tests. *Reference:* scipy.stats.permutation_test with as many resamples as rearrangements (its exact mode) ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.permutation_mc`** — Monte Carlo permutation tests. *Compared:* largest |Δp| between DexVantage and SciPy (9 999 random rearrangements each), in standard errors. *Reference:* scipy.stats.permutation_test with its own random stream ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.bootstrap`** — Bootstrap percentile and BCa intervals. *Compared:* largest endpoint difference in bootstrap standard errors (one sample, paired, two samples). *Reference:* scipy.stats.bootstrap (percentile, BCa) with its own random stream ([efron1993](#ref-efron1993), [scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests)).
- **`stats.multiplicity_bh1995`** — Multiple-comparison corrections (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995 example). *Compared:* rejection-count mismatches plus the largest adjusted-p difference. *Reference:* Benjamini and Hochberg (1995, p. 295) published rejections; Holm and BY written out again here ([benjamini_hochberg1995](#ref-benjamini_hochberg1995), [holm1979](#ref-holm1979), [benjamini_yekutieli2001](#ref-benjamini_yekutieli2001)).
- **`stats.power_cohen1992`** — Sample size against Cohen's power tables. *Compared:* largest |n − n_table| per group over d and h = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8 at alpha 0.01, 0.05, 0.10 (power 0.80). *Reference:* Cohen (1992), "A power primer", Table 2, p. 158 (rows 1 and 5) ([cohen1992](#ref-cohen1992), [cohen1988](#ref-cohen1988)).
- **`stats.power_gpower`** — Power against the G*Power manual's examples. *Compared:* largest power difference over four documented examples (N equal as a further condition). *Reference:* G*Power 3.1 manual, sections 19.3 (p. 48) and 20.3 (p. 50) ([gpower31_manual](#ref-gpower31_manual)).
- **`stats.power_simulation`** — Exact and t-test power against simulation. *Compared:* largest |power − simulated power| in Monte Carlo standard errors. *Reference:* simulated evaluations tested with scipy.stats.fisher_exact, ttest_ind and ttest_rel ([scipy_stats_tests](#ref-scipy_stats_tests), [fleiss2003](#ref-fleiss2003)).
- **`stats.ci_coverage`** — Coverage of the effect-size intervals. *Compared:* largest |coverage − 0.95| in Monte Carlo standard errors (Newcombe: beyond 0.01 for its approximation). *Reference:* simulated normal samples (Cohen's d, noncentral t) and binomial counts (Newcombe risk difference) ([steiger_fouladi1997](#ref-steiger_fouladi1997), [newcombe1998](#ref-newcombe1998)).
- **`stats.bruteforce`** — Rank effect sizes and the detectable difference. *Compared:* largest difference against counting every pair, summing signed ranks in a loop, and power at the detectable difference against the target. *Reference:* brute force written out here; core/stats.power_t and the normal two-proportion power fed back ([cliff1993](#ref-cliff1993)).

### Cluster sweeps (process pool, Slurm shards, shared result cache)

Model `cluster` (dexvantage.core.cluster): 4 of 4 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `cluster.gather_equals_serial` | Gathered shards equal the serial run | 0 | 0 | values | pass |
| `cluster.partition_exact` | Shards cover every item exactly once | 0 | 0 | pairs | pass |
| `cluster.cache_concurrent_writers` | Shared cache: no torn files under concurrent writers | 0 | 0 | reads | pass |
| `cluster.sbatch_directives` | Slurm array script: its #SBATCH lines and bash syntax | 0 | 0 | mismatches | pass |

- **`cluster.gather_equals_serial`** — Gathered shards equal the serial run. *Compared:* numbers and strings that differ between the gathered result of 3 shards and the serial in-process result (a 6-run Latin hypercube and a 6-draw tolerance Monte Carlo on the SO-100 sample), leaving out only how it ran (execution, seconds, cached). *Reference:* the same design and seed run serially in one process (core/experiments.run, the tolerance study) ([slurm_job_array](#ref-slurm_job_array)).
- **`cluster.partition_exact`** — Shards cover every item exactly once. *Compared:* (item count, shard count) pairs, m = 0 … 300 and N = 1 … 40, whose shards do not hold every item exactly once. *Reference:* range(m): every index once (by construction of the definition, counted here).
- **`cluster.cache_concurrent_writers`** — Shared cache: no torn files under concurrent writers. *Compared:* reads that returned a payload other than the one written, plus torn files at the end, with three processes writing and reading the same 24 keys (about 200 kB each) at once. *Reference:* the payload each key was written with (deterministic), compared in full ([rename2](#ref-rename2), [nfs5](#ref-nfs5), [flock2](#ref-flock2)).
- **`cluster.sbatch_directives`** — Slurm array script: its #SBATCH lines and bash syntax. *Compared:* mismatches between the #SBATCH options Slurm would read from the script and the settings given, plus a bash -n failure. *Reference:* the settings given, and bash's own parser ([slurm_sbatch](#ref-slurm_sbatch), [slurm_job_array](#ref-slurm_job_array)).

### Sim-to-real gap (render against recording)

Model `sim2real` (dexvantage.core.sim2real): 7 of 7 checks pass.

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sim2real.emd_vs_scipy` | Histogram EMD against SciPy | 1.72 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | DN | pass |
| `sim2real.mmd_hand_case` | Unbiased MMD² on a case worked by hand | 1.11 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | MMD² (unitless) | pass |
| `sim2real.mmd_gaussians` | Unbiased MMD² against the closed form for two Gaussians | 6.31 × 10⁻⁴ | 0.006751 | MMD² (unitless) | pass |
| `sim2real.noise_known` | Noise σ (Immerkær) on images of known noise | 0.01186 | 0.05 | relative | pass |
| `sim2real.blur_known` | Blur σ that matches the sharpness, on images of known blur | 4.88 × 10⁻⁴ | 0.1 | px | pass |
| `sim2real.shapley_brute_force` | Shapley shares against every order of the corrections | 8.88 × 10⁻¹⁶ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | DN | pass |
| `sim2real.injected_recovery` | Known gaps injected into synthetic recordings, recovered | 0.6783 | 1 | ratio | pass |

- **`sim2real.emd_vs_scipy`** — Histogram EMD against SciPy. *Compared:* largest |EMD − SciPy's Wasserstein-1| over 200 random histogram pairs. *Reference:* scipy.stats.wasserstein_distance on the bin values 0…255 with the histograms as weights ([rubner2000](#ref-rubner2000), [scipy_wasserstein](#ref-scipy_wasserstein)).
- **`sim2real.mmd_hand_case`** — Unbiased MMD² on a case worked by hand. *Compared:* |MMD²_u − its terms written out| for X = {0, 1}, Y = {2, 4}, σ = 1. *Reference:* the estimator's sums by hand ([gretton2012](#ref-gretton2012)).
- **`sim2real.mmd_gaussians`** — Unbiased MMD² against the closed form for two Gaussians. *Compared:* |mean of 400 unbiased estimates − the population MMD²| (4-D Gaussians, RBF σ = 1.5). *Reference:* the closed form E k(X,X') + E k(Y,Y') − 2 E k(X,Y), by eigenvalues; tolerance 4 standard errors ([gretton2012](#ref-gretton2012)).
- **`sim2real.noise_known`** — Noise σ (Immerkær) on images of known noise. *Compared:* largest |σ̂ − σ| / σ over σ = 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 8 DN on a structured image. *Reference:* the σ of the Gaussian noise added (numpy) ([immerkaer1996](#ref-immerkaer1996), [tai_yang2008](#ref-tai_yang2008)).
- **`sim2real.blur_known`** — Blur σ that matches the sharpness, on images of known blur. *Compared:* largest |σ̂ − σ| over σ = 0.8, 1.5 and 3 px. *Reference:* scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter with the σ given (an independent Gaussian blur) ([pech_pacheco2000](#ref-pech_pacheco2000), [scipy_stats](#ref-scipy_stats)).
- **`sim2real.shapley_brute_force`** — Shapley shares against every order of the corrections. *Compared:* largest |φ_i − mean marginal reduction over the 24 orders| for a random cost of four players. *Reference:* brute force over all orders ([shapley1953](#ref-shapley1953)).
- **`sim2real.injected_recovery`** — Known gaps injected into synthetic recordings, recovered. *Compared:* largest recovery error / its tolerance over a brightness offset, a blur, a latency and a mount offset, each alone on the UR5e sample's overhead camera; each must also rank first among the camera's causes. *Reference:* the gaps injected (core/sim2real/inject.py through the synthetic episode generator) ([mujoco_todorov2012](#ref-mujoco_todorov2012), [lerobot_dataset_format](#ref-lerobot_dataset_format), [shapley1953](#ref-shapley1953)).

| Check | Title | Measured | Tolerance | Unit | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `splat.footprint_closed_form` | One Gaussian's footprint against the closed form | 6.16 × 10⁻¹⁵ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | alpha | pass |

| `splat.raster_torch_cuda` | Torch rasteriser (CUDA, float32) against the numpy reference | 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ | 1 × 10⁻⁴ | colour (0–1) | pass |
| `splat.reproject_disparity` | Reprojection between a rectified stereo pair | 1.78 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | px | pass |
| `splat.repose_rigid` | Re-posing a link's Gaussians with the joint state | 5.93 × 10⁻⁷ | 1 × 10⁻⁵ | colour (0–1) | pass |
| `splat.ssim_closed_form` | SSIM and PSNR of constant images against their closed forms | 2.44 × 10⁻¹³ | 1 × 10⁻¹² | SSIM / dB | pass |
| `splat.ssim_vs_skimage` | SSIM against scikit-image | 0 | 1 × 10⁻⁹ | SSIM | pass |

- **`splat.footprint_closed_form`** — One Gaussian's footprint against the closed form. *Compared:* largest |α − o·exp(−½ d²/s²)| over the pixels of one Gaussian on the axis (numpy reference rasteriser). *Reference:* the EWA footprint of an isotropic Gaussian written out: s² = (fσ/z)² + 0.3 px² ([kerbl2023_3dgs](#ref-kerbl2023_3dgs), [zwicker2001_ewa](#ref-zwicker2001_ewa)).
- **`splat.raster_torch_cpu`** — Torch rasteriser (CPU, float64) against the numpy reference. *Compared:* largest colour difference over 300 fixed Gaussians through three lens models. *Reference:* the numpy rasteriser written again without tiles (splat_raster.splat_numpy) ([kerbl2023_3dgs](#ref-kerbl2023_3dgs), [zwicker2001_ewa](#ref-zwicker2001_ewa)).
- **`splat.raster_torch_cuda`** — Torch rasteriser (CUDA, float32) against the numpy reference. *Compared:* largest colour difference over 300 fixed Gaussians through three lens models. *Reference:* the numpy rasteriser written again without tiles, in float64 ([kerbl2023_3dgs](#ref-kerbl2023_3dgs), [zwicker2001_ewa](#ref-zwicker2001_ewa)).
- **`splat.reproject_disparity`** — Reprojection between a rectified stereo pair. *Compared:* largest pixel difference of 500 reprojected points against the closed-form disparity. *Reference:* u_r = u_l − f b / z, v_r = v_l (rectified pinholes) ([kerbl2023_3dgs](#ref-kerbl2023_3dgs)).
- **`splat.repose_rigid`** — Re-posing a link's Gaussians with the joint state. *Compared:* largest colour difference: the rig posed at q against the link-frame Gaussians through the camera moved into the link frame, 5 joint states. *Reference:* the rigid-motion identity render(T · G, C) = render(G, T⁻¹ · C), T from the robot model's link_pose ([qureshi2025_splatsim](#ref-qureshi2025_splatsim), [lou2025_robogs](#ref-lou2025_robogs)).
- **`splat.ssim_closed_form`** — SSIM and PSNR of constant images against their closed forms. *Compared:* largest |SSIM − (2ab + C1)/(a² + b² + C1)| over 40 constant pairs, and |PSNR − (−20 log10 d)|. *Reference:* SSIM's luminance term for constant patches (contrast and structure terms are 1); PSNR's definition ([wang2004_ssim](#ref-wang2004_ssim)).
- **`splat.ssim_vs_skimage`** — SSIM against scikit-image. *Compared:* largest |SSIM − scikit-image's| on the interior of 20 random image pairs. *Reference:* skimage.metrics.structural_similarity (gaussian_weights, σ 1.5, population covariance, data_range 1) ([wang2004_ssim](#ref-wang2004_ssim), [skimage_ssim](#ref-skimage_ssim)).

## How to regenerate

```
dexvantage --validate out/validation
python scripts/gen_validation_doc.py out/validation/validation.json
```

The script refuses a report that is not a full run of the checks registered now, so a new or removed check needs a new run before this page can be made (`tests/test_validation_doc.py` fails until then).
